# Omarchy Network Hub

One Omarchy bar plugin with seven tabs:

- **Overview** - the landing page: what is connected, and where traffic
  actually goes.
- **Network** - the first-party Omarchy Network panel, including Wi-Fi and
  wired Ethernet. Its tab and icon follow the hardware in use.
- **Tailscale** - the first-party Omarchy Tailscale panel.
- **Proton VPN** - jampick's Proton VPN panel, with an added IPv6 route check
  and conservative connection wording.
- **Tor** - TripleU613's Tormarchy panel: system-wide Tor with a real kill
  switch, exit-country selection, new circuits, and live circuit latency.
- **Firewall** - sahzudin's Omawall panel for viewing and managing the UFW
  firewall (status, default policies, and rule add/delete).
- **Ports** - Port Watcher: local socket counts, process details, listeners,
  destination history and quiet evidence-based review items.

The Network tab deliberately keeps the original Omarchy panel layout. Clicking a
tab fades the page content inside one persistent popup. The frame stays open,
and its height eases to fit the next page instead of closing and reopening. `Tab` and
`Shift+Tab` move between pages. On the Firewall page, Tab traverses controls;
Ctrl+Tab and Ctrl+Shift+Tab switch pages. Every page is drawn at the same
width, because the shared tab row is the widest thing in the panel and a page
narrower than the row would clip it. The Overview is a chip rather than a
labelled tab. The wider popup preserves the original *Tailscale*, *Proton*
and *Firewall* labels alongside the new *Ports* tab. On narrow displays the
row falls back to icons with full-name tooltips.

The bar uses the routed physical link icon (Wi-Fi, Ethernet, or disconnected), coloured
by what is carrying your traffic:
green for Proton VPN, blue for Tailscale, split in half when both are up, and
purple for Tor. Tor takes the whole glyph rather than half of it, since it
cannot share a machine with the other two, and it only claims the icon once
traffic is actually going through the circuit - a dimmer purple means Tor is
still bootstrapping.

## Install

```bash
omarchy plugin add https://gitlab.com/Dr.Dj/omarchy_plugin_network_hub.git --enable
omarchy plugin disable omarchy.network
```

The second command replaces the stock Network widget on a fresh Omarchy
installation, avoiding two network icons. Also disable separate
`omarchy.tailscale`, Proton VPN, `tripleu.tor`, and Omawall entries if you had
already enabled those widgets; the hub contains their pages.

The Tor tab needs a one-time privileged setup before it can do anything, and
says so with a **Run setup** button until you have run it:

```bash
sudo ~/.config/omarchy/plugins/drdj.network-hub/tormarchy setup
```

Runtime programs used by the combined panel:

- NetworkManager, `ip`, `iw`, and Omarchy's network helper commands
- `tailscale`
- `protonvpn`, provided by `proton-vpn-cli`
- `python3` for reading Proton's local session cache, the firewall helper and
  Port Watcher; `ss` from `iproute2` supplies its socket readings
- `wl-copy` for copy actions
- `ufw` and `pkexec` (with a working Polkit authentication agent) for the
  Firewall tab
- `nftables`, `systemd`, `polkit`, `curl` and `iproute2` for the Tor tab;
  `tor` itself is installed by that tab's `setup`
- `ip`, `systemctl` and, when present, `resolvectl` for the Overview's probe

Installing Network Hub does not run package hooks or change system services.
The Proton page retains the upstream install button, which asks Omarchy to
install the official Proton CLI and GTK packages only when clicked.

The target Omarchy installation normally supplies the core dependencies.
The Network page checks installed capabilities at startup and when reopened;
missing tools get an explanation, and unavailable DNS/band controls are disabled. Tailscale, Proton VPN and Tor remain optional so installing the hub
does not silently add network services. Each missing optional service has an
explicit setup action in its own tab; the Tailscale action installs the package
and enables `tailscaled`, Proton uses Omarchy's package installer, and Tor keeps
its security-sensitive one-time setup in a visible terminal.

## Wired Ethernet

Ethernet is handled by the same Network page as Wi-Fi. On a wired link the bar
uses the Ethernet glyph, the tab says **Ethernet**, and the page shows the
active interface, negotiated link speed, address, gateway, traffic, latency and
DNS controls. Wi-Fi-only controls (radio toggle, band selector, QR sharing and
access-point list) stay hidden. A wired-only PC therefore never presents a
non-functional Wi-Fi switch.

The Overview resolves its link from the kernel route tables, NetworkManager and
sysfs, so renamed and USB network interfaces do not need hard-coded device
names. On a docked laptop with both Ethernet and Wi-Fi connected, route metrics
select the active physical link. With a VPN route, the bundled probe resolves
the physical underlay instead of mislabelling the tunnel as Ethernet;
Quickshell remains a display fallback. The bar listens for route changes rather
than polling, so switching a dock or route metric updates the shared icon and
tab label too.

## Auto-connect

Both VPN tabs carry an **ON LOGIN** section with a *Connect automatically*
switch (`a` on the keyboard). Both are off by default and are stored on the
widget's `shell.json` entry, so they survive restarts and updates:

```bash
omarchy bar set drdj.network-hub tailscaleAutoConnect true
omarchy bar set drdj.network-hub protonAutoConnect true
omarchy bar set drdj.network-hub protonAutoConnectTarget securecore
```

With one enabled, the widget connects that service once, about six seconds
after the shell starts, and retries a failed attempt every twenty seconds up to
six times - which is what a session that logged in before the network came up
needs. Switching it on while disconnected also connects, rather than waiting
for a login that may be days away.

It only ever connects. It will not sign you in to Proton VPN, will not open a
browser to authorize a Tailscale node, and stops for the rest of the session as
soon as one of these is true:

- the service is connected, by auto-connect or by you
- you turned it off by hand - auto-connect never argues with that
- Proton VPN is signed out, or the Tailscale node has no profile
- the attempts ran out

Switching the setting off and on again re-opens the question; nothing else
does.

`protonAutoConnectTarget` takes any of the panel's quick-connect ids
(`fastest`, `random`, `p2p`, `securecore`, `tor`), or `country:CH` /
`server:CH#1` for somewhere the picker does not offer. An unusable value
connects to the fastest server rather than not connecting at all.

Tailscale's own `tailscaled` service already reconnects on boot; this setting
covers the node that was switched off and should come back on the next login.

## Overview tab

The page the panel opens on. It answers one question before you have clicked
anything: where is my traffic going.

The headline is derived from state, not from the routing table, because with
Tor's ruleset loaded `ip route get` still names your Wi-Fi interface. The
redirect happens in nftables and never touches a route, so a page that printed
the route alone would tell you traffic goes straight out of your NIC while every
TCP connection on the machine is being carried by Tor. The path below it shows
the hops: this machine, the tunnel or circuit carrying it, and where it comes
out. Anything that still goes elsewhere gets its own line, such as the local
networks Tor's Standard mode keeps direct, or tailnet addresses over
`tailscale0`.

Under that, the facts it can read locally: egress interface, DNS servers (or the
note that Tor has taken DNS over), IPv6, what the ruleset drops, and the
firewall. Then one row per service, which jumps to that tab when clicked.

Three things it deliberately does not do:

- **It never escalates.** `bin/net-probe` is unprivileged and never calls
  `pkexec`, because a landing page that opens a password prompt on every panel
  click is not one. The consequence is that the firewall row reports the `ufw`
  unit, not the ruleset. Actual rules need the Firewall tab and its
  authentication.
- **It sends no packets.** The routes come from `ip route get` against
  TEST-NET-1 and the documentation prefix, which is a kernel lookup, so nothing
  here phones a server to ask where you are.
- **It never acts.** No toggles. Each service already solved its own optimistic
  connect state, and a second place to switch things on would be a second place
  to get those races.

It starts no services or duplicate link model of its own either: it reads the
ones the hub already keeps alive for the bar icon, so opening the panel costs
one short probe and nothing else. The probe runs only while the tab is on
screen.

```bash
omarchy bar set drdj.network-hub overviewRefreshIntervalSec 5
```

## Port Watcher tab

The **Ports** tab is a local adaptation of Soham Datta's Port Watcher, pinned
inside this project. It has no runtime dependency on GitHub or an upstream
update feed. This repository owns the adapted collector, evidence rules and UI;
future upstream changes require a deliberate review.

The page shows non-loopback established TCP/UDP connections, processes with
expandable socket/executable details, TCP listeners, unconnected UDP sockets,
and up to 300 recently first-seen remote IPs. Lists show at most 500 rows and
100 endpoints per process; the page indicates truncation. Bind descriptions
say **All interfaces**, **Loopback** or **Interface address**, never claiming
that a listener is reachable through a firewall.

**Listening services** appears near the top, combining TCP listeners and
unconnected UDP sockets, sorted by port. Search by port, protocol, address,
service, process, username, UID, PID or available executable path. Cards show
the systemd unit and owning user; **Details** shows every observed process,
PID, user, available executable path and unit. The socket user and process user
are labelled separately, since they can differ. Units come from observed
cgroups, not guesses based on conventional port numbers.

**Identify system owners** requests a single authenticated, read-only scan
using the trusted system command `pkexec /usr/bin/ss -H -O -lntupe`. All plugin
code stays unprivileged. This reveals protected listener process names and
PIDs; executable paths can still be restricted and are labelled unavailable.
Lookup results are timestamped, held only in memory and joined by address,
protocol, inode and kernel socket cookie. Disappearing or replaced sockets and
visible owner changes invalidate their inspected details. Cancelled or failed
authentication leaves normal monitoring available. Lookups never run
automatically; refresh and background scans do not request authentication.

Review items describe observed evidence, not proof of malware: unfamiliar
executables, shell/relay connections, uncommon ports, temporary/deleted
executables, new destinations/listeners, unusual browser/local ports, fan-out,

# Proton Calendar for Omarchy

A hardened fork of [moorgrove’s original](https://github.com/itsmoorgrove/omarchy-protoncalendar), with a Clock bar mode for replacing the stock clock/calendar widget.

This fork is `0.4.3+drdj.1`, hardened from upstream commit
`515d66def8a7f0b9146251d26dfca9b5feef6b06`. See
[`audit/hardening-summary.txt`](audit/hardening-summary.txt) for changes and tests.
The original source review is preserved in `audit/security-review.txt`.

Your Proton Calendar in the Omarchy bar: what's next, a month grid, a week
grid, and an upcoming list — with a quick add that hands off to the Proton web
app.

![Preview](preview-v2.png)

## What's new in 0.4.3

- The panel notices when the shell is still running a cached older version of
  it after an update, and offers a one-click shell restart
- `Updating` section in the README: `omarchy plugin update` alone is not enough

## What's new in 0.4.2

- The panel closes again. `close()` threw on the bar's read-only
  `centerHoverRevealSuppressed` property and never reached `hide()`, which left
  the panel stuck open and the bar unresponsive (#5, #6)
- A reminder is shown once, not once per monitor. Every bar surface runs its own
  copy of the widget, so a reminder reached the notifier once per screen; the
  notifier now claims each reminder in a lock-guarded state file (#7, #8)
- The reminder sound follows the same claim, so it is heard once per reminder
  burst instead of once per screen, and two reminders due in the same sweep no
  longer play over each other
- Previewing an alarm sound in settings no longer stacks: the most recent click
  wins (#3)
- Event search matches word by word and ignores spacing, so `my company` finds
  `mycompany` and the other way round (#3)

## What's new in 0.4.1

- Complete Swedish localization across weekdays, months, dates, navigation,
  reminders, calendar management, status text, and settings controls
- Language-aware date formatting that follows the plugin language instead of
  the desktop locale

## What's new in 0.4.0

- Full event details with descriptions, locations, participants, organizers,
  recurrence status, source time zones, and one-click meeting links
- A focused day view plus search and `All`, `Today`, and `Week` filters
- Multiple reminders, all-day reminders, per-calendar alert defaults, and
  notification actions for opening, snoozing, and dismissing
- Share links migrate from `feeds.json` into Secret Service when available
- Per-calendar visibility, order, name, color, sync status, and notification controls
- Six bar modes including countdown, current event, today count, and privacy
- Richer quick add with end time, calendar, location, and private clipboard handoff
- English and Swedish UI, 12/24-hour clocks, secondary time zones, and optional week numbers

## What's new in 0.3.0

- Choose Sunday or Monday as the first day of the week from the settings panel

## What's new in 0.2.0

- Desktop notifications one hour before timed events by default
- Global reminder presets, custom minutes, and per-event overrides
- Optional alarm sound with four live-preview choices
- One-minute notification test directly from the settings panel
- Official Proton Calendar icon in desktop notifications
- A cleaner, aligned notification settings layout

## What it does, and what it can't

Proton Calendar has no CalDAV and no public write API. Reading works well:
the plugin fetches your calendar's share link (plain iCalendar over HTTPS),
expands recurring events, and caches the result. Writing is a handover —
quick add copies the title to your clipboard and opens the Proton web app on
the right day, but you finish the event in the browser.

This version keeps event details out of the browser URL and marks copied
text as sensitive, serving it for one paste. Clipboard managers must honor the
sensitive hint to exclude it from history; this does not isolate the clipboard
from other applications in your desktop session.

Calendar requests require HTTPS and go directly to the destination, ignoring
curl configuration and proxy environment variables. VPN routing still applies.
The private-host test override permits HTTP only for loopback fixtures.
Removing a calendar clears its ICS cache and refreshes the event cache; keyring
deletion failures are reported. Syncs and feed edits use a shared lock.

The share link is a secret URL — anyone holding it can read that calendar,
and its contents are no longer end-to-end encrypted the way the rest of your
Proton data is.

## Requirements

```bash
sudo pacman -S --needed python-icalendar python-recurring-ical-events wl-clipboard libsecret libnotify
```

`python-icalendar` and `python-recurring-ical-events` are required for the
plugin to work at all — without them it can't parse your calendar feed.
`wl-clipboard` is needed for the quick-add clipboard handover.
`libsecret` stores share links in the desktop keyring, while `libnotify`
provides actionable reminders. If Secret Service is unavailable, the plugin
keeps the link in an owner-only `feeds.json` without deleting it.

## Install

```bash
omarchy plugin add https://gitlab.com/Dr.Dj/omarchy_plugin_protoncalendar.git
```

The plugin ID is `drdj.protoncalendar`. Its Clock mode displays the date and time;
other modes show upcoming events or privacy status.

Then open the panel and paste your calendar's share link (Proton Calendar →
Settings → Calendars → your calendar → Share → Share with anyone).

## Updating

```bash
omarchy restart shell
```

```bash
omarchy plugin update drdj.protoncalendar
omarchy restart shell
```

Maintain this fork's security changes when merging commits from the original upstream.

The restart is not optional. Omarchy reloads a plugin's bar widget when the
files change, but the panel QML stays in the QML engine's in-memory component
cache, so the old code keeps running until the shell is restarted — a fixed
panel can still behave like the broken one, and the shell log keeps reporting
errors against line numbers from the version you just replaced.

From 0.4.3 the panel notices this itself: it compares the version compiled into
it against `manifest.json` on disk, and if they disagree it shows a notice with
a restart button. That check can only run once the new code is loaded, so the
update *into* 0.4.3 still needs the restart above.

## Features

- **Bar mark** — pips for how much is on today, a warning colour when a feed
  is stale, and the next event's title beside it
- **Month** — always six rows, ISO week numbers, today outlined, up to four
  event dots per day
- **Week** — an hour grid with an all-day band, overlapping events side by
  side, a line for right now, and a Sunday or Monday week start
- **Day** — one spacious timeline focused on the selected day
- **Upcoming** — everything ahead as one dated list, grouped by month
- **Event details** — description, location, attendees, organizer, recurrence,
  source and secondary time zones, plus meeting and Proton actions
- **Search** — text search across event content with today and week scopes
- **Quick add** — start/end time, all-day, calendar, and location handoff to Proton
- **Multiple calendars** — reorder, rename, recolor, hide, pause, and configure alerts
- **Notifications** — multiple lead times, all-day and per-calendar defaults,
  per-event overrides, sounds, snooze, dismiss, and a built-in test
- **Privacy** — keyring-backed share links and a bar mode that never exposes titles

The plugin sends standard freedesktop notification actions. Omarchy currently
uses a notification-card click for the default `Open in Proton` action; snooze
controls are always available from the event detail card even when the active
notification theme does not render secondary action buttons.

## Keyboard

| Key | Action |

| `←`/`→` or `[`/`]` | Previous / next month or week |
| `↑`/`↓` or `{`/`}` | Previous / next year or four weeks |
| `t` / `enter` | Back to today |
| `m` / `e` / `u` | Month / week / upcoming |

| `n` / `a` | New event |
| `o` | Open the selected day in Proton |
| `r` | Refresh |
| `w` | Toggle week start |
| `esc` | Close |

Right-click the bar widget to cycle the bar label; middle-click to refresh.

## Settings

| Key | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `refreshIntervalSec` | integer | 900 | Feed poll interval |
| `barMode` | enum | `Countdown` | `Off`, `Next event`, `Countdown`, `Today count`, `Current event`, or `Privacy` |
| `defaultView` | enum | `Month` | `Month`, `Week`, `Day`, or `Upcoming` |
| `weekStartDay` | enum | `Sunday` | `Sunday` or `Monday` |
| `language` | enum | `System` | `System`, `English`, or `Swedish` |
| `timeFormat` | enum | `System` | `System`, `24-hour`, or `12-hour` |
| `secondaryTimeZone` | timezone | — | Optional IANA zone such as `Europe/London` or `UTC` |
| `showWeekNumbers` | boolean | `true` | Show ISO week numbers in month view |
| `dayStartHour` | integer | 7 | Week view window start |
| `dayEndHour` | integer | 22 | Week view window end |
| `quickAddDurationMinutes` | integer | 60 | Default quick-add event duration |
| `notificationsEnabled` | boolean | `true` | Desktop notifications for timed events |
| `notificationSoundEnabled` | boolean | `true` | Alarm sound with event notifications |
| `notificationSound` | enum | `Alarm` | `Gentle`, `Bell`, `Chime`, or `Alarm` |
| `reminderMinutes` | integer | 60 | Default notification lead time |
| `reminderMinutesList` | integer list | `[60]` | One or more notification lead times |
| `allDayNotificationsEnabled` | boolean | `false` | Desktop notifications for all-day events |
| `allDayReminderDays` | integer | 1 | Days before an all-day event |
| `allDayReminderHour` | integer | 9 | Local hour for all-day notifications |
| `feedsFile` | path | — | Defaults to `~/.config/omarchy/protoncalendar/feeds.json` |

## Tests

`test/run` exercises the backend and `Model.js` against a synthetic
iCalendar fixture — all-day events, multi-day spans, recurrence, and a
daily rule crossing the autumn DST change.

```bash
bash audit/run-security-checks --upstream-tests
bash audit/run-security-checks
```

The audit runner uses `bwrap`, Node, and an isolated Python environment with
`icalendar` and `recurring-ical-events`. Set `PROTONCAL_REVIEW_PYTHON` to that
environment's Python. The runner overlays the desktop home and disables external
networking; the test helper fixes the sync date to match the dated ICS fixtures.

## Removal

```bash
omarchy plugin remove drdj.protoncalendar
rm -rf ~/.config/omarchy/protoncalendar ~/.cache/omarchy/protoncalendar
```

https://gitlab.com/akacross/sampcmd.readme_excerpt:
# sampcmd — a robust SA:MP launcher for Windows and Wine/Proton

A modern rewrite of `sampcmd.exe`. It launches `gta_sa.exe`, injects `samp.dll`,
and — unlike the original — validates and logs **every** stage so a failure can
never pass silently. It is designed to behave identically on native Windows and
under Wine / Proton / UMU / Lutris / Steam.

## Why the rewrite

The original launcher assumed native Windows behavior and reported success even
when injection failed. Under Wine/Proton the symptom was: `gta_sa.exe` launches,
exits immediately, and the launcher still returns `0`.

This version fixes the correctness bugs from the original and, importantly, two
things the surface-level analysis missed:

1. **It is built 32-bit.** `gta_sa.exe` and `samp.dll` are PE32/i386. A 64-bit
   launcher cannot `CreateRemoteThread` + `LoadLibraryW` into a 32-bit process.
   The build fails loudly if pointed at a 64-bit toolchain.

2. **It sets the child's working directory to the game folder.** GTA:SA exits
   instantly if its current directory isn't the game directory, and under
   Steam/Proton/UMU the inherited cwd usually isn't. The original passed
   `lpCurrentDirectory = NULL` and resolved paths from `GetCurrentDirectory()`;
   this version anchors everything to the launcher's own `.exe` location.

### Correctness fixes carried over from the analysis

- `STARTUPINFOW.cb` is initialized (Wine is stricter than Windows).
- The remote `LoadLibraryW` thread's **exit code (the returned `HMODULE`) is
  checked**; `0` means the DLL did not load, and that is reported, not ignored.
- `VirtualAllocEx` uses `PAGE_READWRITE` (the injected path is data, not code).
- `VirtualAllocEx` result, `WriteProcessMemory` byte count, and the located
  `LoadLibraryW` address are all validated.
- All handles and remote allocations use RAII wrappers (no leaks on any path).
- The command line handed to GTA is **rebuilt** with `gta_sa.exe` as `argv[0]`
  rather than forwarding `sampcmd`'s own command line verbatim.
- `std::filesystem` for all path handling; Unicode throughout.
- Runtime Wine/Proton detection (`wine_get_version`, env markers) — logged.

## Architecture

```
main            -> App (orchestrator)
App             -> Cli, Logger, Diagnostics, WineDetection,
                   ProcessLauncher, Injector, Monitor, ErrorFormatter
Win32Helpers    -> ScopedHandle / RemoteMemory RAII + error formatting
```

One file per module under `src/`.

## Build (Linux -> Windows PE, 32-bit)

Requires the MinGW-w64 i686 toolchain:

```sh
sudo pacman -S mingw-w64-gcc      # Arch / CachyOS
# or: sudo apt install g++-mingw-w64-i686 cmake
```

Then:

```sh
./build.sh                                   # -> build/sampcmd.exe
./build.sh --deploy "/path/to/GTA San Andreas 0.3.7"   # backs up the original first
```

Or manually:

```sh
cmake -B build -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=cmake/toolchain-mingw-i686.cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build --parallel
```

(On native Windows, configure with any 32-bit MSVC/MinGW generator instead.)

## Usage

```
sampcmd [launcher-options] [--] [gta_sa.exe arguments...]
```

The launcher's own options use `--long` form; single-dash flags and everything
else are forwarded to `gta_sa.exe`, so the existing SA:MP invocation still works:

```sh
sampcmd -c -n MyNick -h 127.0.0.1 -p 7777
```

### open.mp

Pass `-omp` to also inject `omp-client.dll` (from the game folder) **after**
`samp.dll` — open.mp layers on top of an already-loaded samp.dll. The connection
flags are unchanged; `-omp` is consumed by the launcher and not forwarded to GTA.
It may appear **anywhere** on the command line — including after `--` — so it can
sit alongside the connect flags.

```sh
sampcmd -omp -c -n MyNick -h 127.0.0.1 -p 7777
# custom path: sampcmd -omp --omp-dll "C:\path\to\omp-client.dll" -c -n ... -h ... -p ...
```

### Hostnames in `-h` (dead DNS pool members)

If `-h` is a hostname rather than an IP, sampcmd resolves it and forwards **an
address the server actually answers on**.

This exists because of a failure that looks nothing like DNS. SA:MP connects to
the *first* address the resolver hands it, and community servers publish
round-robin A-record pools whose members outlive the machines behind them. Wine
resolves through `getaddrinfo`, whose RFC 3484 ordering is stable for a given
client — so if the dead member sorts first you do not get an intermittent
failure, you get `Failed to connect to host` on every single attempt, on a
hostname that looks perfectly healthy everywhere else.

Resolving alone does not fix it (the stock `samp.exe` resolves too, and picks
the same dead address), so sampcmd **proves** the address first: it sends the
same info query a server browser sends and takes the first candidate that
answers.

```
[Host resolve]
host           : s2.gta-mp.cz (port 7777)
resolved       : 8 address(es)
  178.32.234.16  - no reply in 700 ms (attempt 1 of 3)
  51.254.21.27   - answered in 117 ms  <- using this
WARN 1 address(es) ahead of 51.254.21.27 did not answer - the DNS pool has dead members
```

Cost is one UDP round-trip (~120–250 ms) in the normal case, since the first
address usually answers. It never makes things worse: an IP literal, a missing
`-h`, a resolver failure, or a pool where nothing answers all fall back to
forwarding the hostname exactly as before.

#### One query is not proof — retries and `sampcmd.hosts`

A SA:MP query is a single UDP datagram with no retransmission, and real servers
drop them. Measured 2026-08-16, 20 queries per run, paced and unpaced:

| server | address | answered | RTT |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `samp.hzgaming.net` | 213.32.6.232 | 17/20, 18/20 | ~118 ms |
| `s2.gta-mp.cz` | 51.254.21.27 | 20/20 | ~118 ms |

So hzgaming — a live server with a *single* A record, answering in a sixth of the
probe timeout — looked dead about one launch in seven, and the launcher then
logged `no address answered a SA:MP query` and forwarded the hostname. Nothing
was wrong with the timeout; the packet simply never came back.

Two things follow. The probe now walks the pool **three times** instead of once,
which takes a false "dead" from ~1/7 to ~1/350 for that server and costs nothing
when an address answers. And every proven address is written to
**`sampcmd.hosts`**, next to the log:

```
# host <tab> port <tab> address <tab> proven-at <tab> rtt_ms <tab> fails <tab> pool
samp.hzgaming.net	7777	213.32.6.232	1786915058	118	0	213.32.6.232
```

That file is used four ways:

- **Tried first.** The address that answered last time goes to the head of the
  probe queue, so a bad DNS order costs nothing after the first launch.
- **Trusted for 5 minutes.** Relaunching the server you were just on (usually
  after a crash) skips DNS and the probe entirely — `cache hit : 213.32.6.232 -
  answered 15 s ago in 118 ms; skipping DNS and probe`.
- **Fallback for a day.** If nothing answers this launch but this host answered
  within the last 24 hours *and* DNS still lists that address, it is used anyway
  — silence is far more likely to be a dropped datagram than a dead server. After
  3 such launches with no fresh proof, the entry is forgotten.
- **Survives a DNS outage.** If the name stops resolving, the addresses from the
  last successful lookup are probed instead of giving up.

Add a line by hand to pin a host permanently — no DNS, no probe, no expiry:

```
myserver.net	7777	203.0.113.10	pin
```

`--host-cache <path>` moves the file; `--no-host-cache` disables reading and
writing it.

### Diagnosing the "exits immediately" problem

```sh
# 1. Prove the launcher's view of the world (no launch):
sampcmd --dry-run --debug --console -- -c -n MyNick -h 127.0.0.1 -p 7777

# 2. Does GTA start at all without SA:MP?
sampcmd --no-inject -- -c -n MyNick -h 127.0.0.1 -p 7777

# 3. Full launch with a complete trace:
sampcmd --debug -- -c -n MyNick -h 127.0.0.1 -p 7777
cat "sampcmd.log"   # written next to sampcmd.exe, named after the launcher
```

If injection fails, the log and an error dialog name the exact stage
(`LoadLibraryW returned NULL inside gta_sa.exe`, etc.) instead of GTA vanishing.

## Runtime monitoring (what happened after launch)

The launcher stays attached after starting GTA and reports how the process
behaved. Two tiers:

- **Startup watchdog (default).** Waits a grace window (`--grace`, default 8s) for
  an early exit. If GTA exits/crashes, it decodes the exit status (e.g.
  `0xC0000005 ACCESS_VIOLATION`, `0xC0000135 DLL_NOT_FOUND`) and prints a report.
  If GTA is still healthy after the window, the launcher detaches.
- **`--monitor` / `--gdb` (gdb-lite).** Attaches the Win32 debug API for the whole
  session and additionally captures the **faulting module + offset**, the
  exception chain, the loaded-module list (incl. whether `samp.dll` loaded), and
  the game's own `OutputDebugString` output. Add `--watch` to a plain run to stay
  attached without the debugger.

The report is a compact, delimited block designed to be **pasted back for
debugging**:

```
===== SAMPCMD REPORT (copy everything between the lines) =====
sampcmd     : 2.4.1
os / wine   : 10.0.19045 | Wine 11.12 (Linux 6.x)
target      : gta_sa.exe [samp.dll injected]
outcome     : CRASHED after 2140 ms
exit/status : 0xC0000005  ACCESS_VIOLATION (bad memory access)
fault       : 0xC0000005 ACCESS_VIOLATION at gta_sa.exe+0x28A1B2
exceptions  : 2 seen (showing the fatal one)
modules     : 41 loaded | samp.dll LOADED
output@fault:
  > SA-MP: ...
  ... then:
  > SA-MP: ...
omitted     : 37 mirrored plugin log line(s), e.g. cleo.asi (--all-output keeps them)
log file    : Z:\...\sampcmd.log
===== END REPORT =====
```

### Crashes: SA-MP's dialog, its text, and a dump (2.4)

A debugger being attached is exactly what makes Windows and Wine skip a
program's own unhandled-exception filter, so under `--monitor` SA-MP's crash
dialog used to never appear: the fault came to sampcmd instead, and sampcmd
ended the game.

Now, at the **first hard fault** (an access violation, an illegal instruction -
`0xC0000xxx`), while the faulting thread is still stopped on it, sampcmd:

1. reads its registers and stack and writes **what SA-MP's crash dialog shows**,
   in samp.dll's own format (`Exception At Address`, `Base`, the registers,
   `EFLAGS`, the 0x280 bytes of stack, and for 0.3.7-R5 `SCM Op / lDbg /
   LastRendObj` and `Game Version`), into the log and the report;
2. lists the **code addresses on that stack** as `module+offset` - the likely
   callers, which the dialog never named. Modules are named from the loader's
   own list read at the fault (2.4.1): Wine loads, unloads and reloads some
   DLLs at one base, and a record kept from the load events alone named
   whole ranges after a DLL that had left;
3. writes a **minidump** next to the log, `sampcmd-crash-<date>-<time>.dmp`
   (the faulting thread's registers and stack, the module list, the code
   around the fault; the newest five are kept). `--full-dump` writes the
   game's whole memory instead (hundreds of MB to a few GB; the newest two are
   kept) - what a heap corrupted earlier needs. `--no-dump` writes none.
4. **lets go of the game** (`DebugActiveProcessStop` with the exception still
   pending), so the fault is dispatched as if no debugger had been there: the
   game's own handlers, then SA-MP's crash dialog. sampcmd waits for the game
   to end and reports its exit status. A fault the game handles just carries
   on, unwatched for the rest of the session.

`--no-crash-dialog` keeps the 2.3 behaviour: stay attached, and end the game
once the fault proves unhandled (steps 1-3 still happen).

The report then carries, after the fault line:

```
handed over : sampcmd let go at the fault so the game's own crash handler (SA-MP's dialog) could run
dump        : S:\Games\samp-0.3.7\sampcmd-crash-20261012-023521.dmp (2.4 MB)
code on the stack (nearest the fault first):
  +000C  d3d9.dll+0x1A5F80
  ...
SA-MP crash info:
  SA-MP 0.3.7-R5
  Exception At Address: 0x623E63E9

# ProtonMail IMAP/SMTP Bridge Docker Container

![version badge](https://img.shields.io/docker/v/shenxn/protonmail-bridge)
![image size badge](https://img.shields.io/docker/image-size/shenxn/protonmail-bridge/build)
![docker pulls badge](https://img.shields.io/docker/pulls/shenxn/protonmail-bridge)
![deb badge](https://github.com/shenxn/protonmail-bridge-docker/workflows/pack%20from%20deb/badge.svg)
![build badge](https://github.com/shenxn/protonmail-bridge-docker/workflows/build%20from%20source/badge.svg)

This is an unofficial Docker container of the [ProtonMail Bridge](https://protonmail.com/bridge/). Some of the scripts are based on [Hendrik Meyer's work](https://gitlab.com/T4cC0re/protonmail-bridge-docker).

Docker Hub: [https://hub.docker.com/r/shenxn/protonmail-bridge](https://hub.docker.com/r/shenxn/protonmail-bridge)

GitHub: [https://github.com/shenxn/protonmail-bridge-docker](https://github.com/shenxn/protonmail-bridge-docker)

## ARM Support

We now support ARM devices (`arm64` and `arm/v7`)! Use the images tagged with `build`. See next section for details.

## Tags

There are two types of images.
 - `deb`: Images based on the official [.deb release](https://protonmail.com/bridge/install). It only supports the `amd64` architecture.
 - `build`: Images based on the [source code](https://github.com/ProtonMail/proton-bridge). It supports `amd64`, `arm64`, `arm/v7` and `riscv64`. Supporting to more architectures is possible. PRs are welcome.

tag | description
 -- | --
`latest` | latest `deb` image
`[version]` | `deb` images
`build` | latest `build` image
`[version]-build` | `build` images

## Initialization

To initialize and add account to the bridge, run the following command.

```
docker run --rm -it -v protonmail:/root shenxn/protonmail-bridge init
```

If you want to use Docker Compose instead, you can create a copy of the provided example [docker-compose.yml](docker-compose.yml) file, modify it to suit your needs, and then run the following command:

```
docker compose run protonmail-bridge init
```

Wait for the bridge to startup, then you will see a prompt appear for [Proton Mail Bridge interactive shell](https://proton.me/support/bridge-cli-guide). Use the `login` command and follow the instructions to add your account into the bridge. Then use `info` to see the configuration information (username and password). After that, use `exit` to exit the bridge. You may need `CTRL+C` to exit the docker entirely.

## Run

To run the container, use the following command.

```
docker run -d --name=protonmail-bridge -v protonmail:/root -p 1025:25/tcp -p 1143:143/tcp --restart=unless-stopped shenxn/protonmail-bridge
```

Or, if using Docker Compose, use the following command.

```
docker compose up -d
```

## Kubernetes

If you want to run this image in a Kubernetes environment. You can use the [Helm](https://helm.sh/) chart (https://github.com/k8s-at-home/charts/tree/master/charts/stable/protonmail-bridge) created by [@Eagleman7](https://github.com/Eagleman7). More details can be found in [#23](https://github.com/shenxn/protonmail-bridge-docker/issues/23).

If you don't want to use Helm, you can also reference to the guide ([#6](https://github.com/shenxn/protonmail-bridge-docker/issues/6)) written by [@ghudgins](https://github.com/ghudgins).

## Security

Please be aware that running the command above will expose your bridge to the network. Remember to use firewall if you are going to run this in an untrusted network or on a machine that has public IP address. You can also use the following command to publish the port to only localhost, which is the same behavior as the official bridge package.

```
docker run -d --name=protonmail-bridge -v protonmail:/root -p 127.0.0.1:1025:25/tcp -p 127.0.0.1:1143:143/tcp --restart=unless-stopped shenxn/protonmail-bridge
```

Besides, you can publish only port 25 (SMTP) if you don't need to receive any email (e.g. as a email notification service).

## Compatibility

The bridge currently only supports some of the email clients. More details can be found on the official website. I've tested this on a Synology DiskStation and it runs well. However, you may need ssh onto it to run the interactive docker command to add your account. The main reason of using this instead of environment variables is that it seems to be the best way to support two-factor authentication.

## Bridge CLI Guide

The initialization step exposes the bridge CLI so you can do things like switch between combined and split mode, change proxy, etc. The [official guide](https://protonmail.com/support/knowledge-base/bridge-cli-guide/) gives more information on to use the CLI.

## Build

For anyone who want to build this container on your own (for development or security concerns), here is the guide to do so. First, you need to `cd` into the directory (`deb` or `build`, depending on which type of image you want). Then just run the docker build command
```
docker build .
```

That's it. The `Dockerfile` and bash scripts handle all the downloading, building, and packing. You can also add tags, push to your favorite docker registry, or use `buildx` to build multi architecture images.

# Proton Bridge Free

An unofficial Proton Mail bridge for free accounts. Runs a local IMAP/SMTP server so standard email clients (Thunderbird, Apple Mail, etc.) can work with Proton Mail.

> **⚠️ Work in Progress** — This project is in early development.

## What it does

- Authenticates with Proton Mail using your existing account
- Decrypts messages locally using OpenPGP
- Exposes a local IMAP server (default: `localhost:1143`) for reading mail
- Exposes a local SMTP server (default: `localhost:1025`) for sending mail
- Caches message metadata locally in SQLite for fast access

## Building

```bash
go build ./cmd/proton-bridge-free
```

## Usage

```bash
./proton-bridge-free --imap-port 1143 --smtp-port 1025
```

On first run, you'll be prompted for your Proton Mail credentials.

Then configure your email client:
- IMAP: `localhost:1143`
- SMTP: `localhost:1025`
- Username/password: the bridge password shown during setup

## Development

See [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) for the full development guide, and [docs/AGENTS.md](docs/AGENTS.md) for multi-agent development workflow.

## License

MIT

## Disclaimer

This is an unofficial project and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or associated with Proton AG. Use at your own risk. Proton's API is not publicly documented and may change without notice.

https://gitlab.com/xarif/docker/protonma.readme_excerpt:
# protonmail-bridge

Self-built, self-owned [Proton Mail Bridge](https://proton.me/mail/bridge) image —
a headless SMTP/IMAP relay that lets in-cluster apps send mail through a Proton
Mail account. Built from the official
[ProtonMail/proton-bridge](https://github.com/ProtonMail/proton-bridge) sources,
**not** a wrapper around a third-party image.

- **Registry (pull source)**: `registry.gitlab.com/xarif/docker/protonmail-bridge` — the
  cluster pulls from the gitlab.com mirror. Forgejo's registry binds each tagged manifest
  to a DB row keyed by the tag instead of storing it content-addressably, so re-pushing a
  rolling tag deletes the old manifest and turns any digest pin into `MANIFEST_UNKNOWN`
  (this bit the deployment once already). The external mirror also keeps the mail path
  pullable while Forgejo or the cluster is down.
- **Registry (Forgejo-side build)**: `git.xarif.de/docker/protonmail-bridge` — the
  same `dagger call … ci` build (one digest on both registries), tags `main` + `latest`, not
  consumed by the cluster.
- **Consumed by**: [kubernetes/smtp-server 🌐](https://git.xarif.de/kubernetes/smtp-server)

## Why self-built

The previous image wrapped the community `shenxn/protonmail-bridge` image and
only added `libfido2`. That image lagged upstream and — more importantly — the
bridge **silently self-updated over the internet at runtime**, so the version we
pinned in Git was not the version actually running. This image inverts that:

- **We own the build.** The bridge is compiled from a pinned source tag
  (`make build-nogui`, no Qt/GUI). The version is controlled by the `version`
  build arg, bumped by **Renovate** (GitHub releases of `ProtonMail/proton-bridge`)
  → CI rebuilds → the Kubernetes repo picks up the new digest. Updates are a
  reviewable, auditable Git change, not an opaque runtime download.
- **Auto-update disabled** (two layers): the bridge binaries are made read-only
  at build time (`chmod -w`) so the self-updater physically cannot replace them,
  and the entrypoint additionally sets `AutoUpdate=false` in the vault so it does
  not even try.
- **Telemetry disabled.** The entrypoint sets `TelemetryDisabled=true` in the
  vault (usage diagnostics are on by default upstream).
- **Robust long-uptime operation.** The bridge is kept alive with
  `sleep infinity > faketty` instead of the fragile `cat faketty |` pipe, which
  detaches after long uptimes and crashes the moment anything closes the FIFO.

## How settings are applied without the interactive CLI

Proton Bridge stores its settings in an encrypted `vault.enc`. There is no ENV
or flag to configure it — only the interactive CLI, which is fragile to drive in
a container. Instead we build the official **`vault-editor`** debug tool
(`make ... vault-editor`), which reads/writes the vault as JSON. Before the
bridge starts (while the vault is unlocked), the entrypoint runs:

```sh
vault-editor read \
  | jq '.Settings.TelemetryDisabled = true
      | .Settings.AutoUpdate = false
      | .Settings.MaxSyncMemory = 268435456' \
  | vault-editor write
```

`MaxSyncMemory` is capped at 256 MiB — the upstream default is **2 GiB**, far
above the container's memory limit, so an uncapped mailbox re-sync is a latent
OOMKill of the whole mail relay. 256 MiB stays well under the limit and is ample
for a low-volume account.

This is idempotent, schema-validated (jq aborts on an unexpected shape), and
fault-tolerant (a failure is logged but never blocks the relay from starting).

## Build

Multi-stage (`build/Dockerfile`):

- **build stage** — `debian:sid-slim` (its apt Go is new enough for the bridge's
  `go.mod`; the build stage is never shipped). Shallow-clones the pinned tag and
  runs `make build-nogui vault-editor`.
- **runtime stage** — `debian:bookworm-slim` + only runtime deps
  (`socat pass gnupg libsecret-1-0 libfido2-1 ca-certificates procps jq`).

Local build/test (the CI call, never publishes); `mise run image` builds and loads the
image into the local Docker engine as `xarif-protonmail-bridge`:

```sh
mise run pipeline
```

## Initialization

Credentials are entered interactively once and persist in the volume/PVC
(`/root`); they are not stored as a secret. In Kubernetes:

```sh
kubectl exec -it -n protonmail deployment/bridge -- bash /protonmail/entrypoint.sh init
```

Use `login` to authenticate, `info` to view the SMTP/IMAP credentials, then
`exit`. The `init` path kills any running bridge instance first, so it works
inside an already-running container.

## Optional: encrypt the credential keyring

By default the GPG key backing the `pass` store has no passphrase, so anyone
with the volume can recover the credentials. Set `KEYRING_PASSPHRASE` (e.g. from
a SOPS secret) to protect it. On first `init` the key is generated with the
passphrase; at every start `setup_gpg_passphrase()` presets it into `gpg-agent`
so the bridge decrypts unattended.

**Adopting this on an existing (unprotected) setup — no re-authentication needed.**
The `pass` store and `vault.enc` are encrypted with the *public* key, which does
not change when you add a passphrase to the *private* key, so the existing
credentials stay valid. After setting `KEYRING_PASSPHRASE` in the environment,
protect the existing key in place (GnuPG 2.2, verified):

```sh
# In the running container. An unprotected key has no OLD passphrase, so the
# NEW one must be supplied via --passphrase-fd (NOT --command-fd, which is a no-op here).
printf '%s' "$KEYRING_PASSPHRASE" | gpg --batch --pinentry-mode loopback \
    --passphrase-fd 0 --change-passphrase pass-key
```

Then restart the container so `setup_gpg_passphrase()` presets the passphrase
against the now-protected key. Re-running `init` (which regenerates the key and
forces re-authentication) is only needed if the key/pass store is being recreated
from scratch.

## Configuration reference

| Setting | Value | How |
|---|---|---|
| Bridge version | pinned `version` build arg | Renovate (github-releases) |
| Auto-update | disabled | read-only binaries + vault `AutoUpdate=false` |
| Telemetry | disabled | vault `TelemetryDisabled=true` |
| Sync memory cap | 256 MiB (default 2 GiB) | vault `MaxSyncMemory` — kept under the container mem limit |
| SMTP | `:25` (STARTTLS) | socat → bridge `:1025` |
| IMAP | **not exposed** | bridge serves `127.0.0.1:1143`, but the entrypoint does not forward `:143` |
| Keyring passphrase | off unless `KEYRING_PASSPHRASE` set | opt-in |

## Renovate

`renovate.json` extends `local>infra/renovate-config`. Renovate keeps current:
the `version` build arg (Proton Bridge GitHub releases) and the base-image
digests. New releases open a PR; on merge CI rebuilds and publishes.

## Known limitations / future work

- **Runs as root.** The bridge needs a writable `/root` (config/cache/vault) and
  socat binds privileged ports 25/143. The Kubernetes deployment hardens this
  (`drop: [ALL]` + `add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE]`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`,
  `seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault`). Running fully non-root would require moving
  the vault off `/root` (PVC migration + re-login) and is deferred.

## Credits

Build approach adapted from [shenxn/protonmail-bridge-docker](https://github.com/shenxn/protonmail-bridge-docker)
and the actively maintained fork [dancwilliams/protonmail-bridge-docker](https://github.com/dancwilliams/protonmail-bridge-docker)
(read-only auto-update backstop, `sleep infinity` FIFO fix, GPG socket cleanup).

# proton-ff11-ime

Linux の Steam で FINAL FANTASY XI を遊ぶときに、日本語入力（fcitx5 + Mozc などの XIM）を使えるようにした Proton です。

Valve 公式の Proton Experimental に、Wine の日本語入力まわりの修正（`dlls/imm32`、`dlls/winex11.drv`）だけを加えています。

> 非公式の改変版です。Valve Corporation およびスクウェア・エニックスとは関係ありません。

*An unofficial Proton build with Japanese input method (XIM) fixes for FINAL FANTASY XI on Linux. Not affiliated with Valve or Square Enix.*

## 直るもの

- 変換中の文字の表示と、確定した文字の入力
- 変換の途中で続けて打ったときに、変換中の文字が消える問題
- 全角/半角キーを押したときに、入力途中の文字が確定されない問題
- 起動直後に英数字が入力できない問題
- Backspace が2文字消える問題
- NumLock がオンの環境で、キー入力のたびに NumLock キーが押されたことになる問題

## 使い方

1. このプロジェクトの「リリース」ページ（Deploy → Releases）から `proton-ff11-ime-<版>.tar.gz` をダウンロードします。
2. Steam の互換ツールフォルダに展開します。
   ```
   mkdir -p ~/.steam/root/compatibilitytools.d
   tar -xf proton-ff11-ime-<版>.tar.gz -C ~/.steam/root/compatibilitytools.d
   ```
3. Steam を再起動します。
4. ライブラリで FF11 のショートカットを右クリック →「プロパティ」→「互換性」で、**Proton FF11 (IME patched)** を選びます。

必要なもの：

- XIM に対応したインプットメソッド（fcitx5 + Mozc で確認）
- `XMODIFIERS=@im=fcitx` などの設定と、日本語ロケール（デスクトップで設定されていれば、Steam 経由でゲームにも渡ります）

FF11 を Steam の「非 Steam ゲーム」として追加する方法などは、次の記事で詳しく説明しています。

- [Linux で FFXI（日本語版）を遊ぶ（Steam 版）— Proton で日本語入力まで（note）](https://note.com/kagetaro078/n/n5d5349606b5c)

ゲームのインストールは、ここには含まれていません。

## 自分でビルドする

Docker と、Proton 公式の SDK イメージを使います。

```
git clone https://github.com/ValveSoftware/wine.git wine
git -C wine checkout <Release に書いてある Wine のコミット>
git -C wine am ../proton-ff11-ime.patch
./build.sh                      # out/ に imm32.dll と winex11.so（32bit/64bit）ができます
PROTON_SRC=<同じ版の Proton Experimental のフォルダ> ./make_dist.sh 1
```

`make_dist.sh` は、Proton Experimental のフォルダを複製して `out/` の4ファイルを差し替え、`dist/` に tar.gz を作ります。

## ライセンス

- パッチとスクリプト：LGPL 2.1 以降（`LICENSE`、Wine と同じ）
- 配布物に含まれる Proton 本体とその部品は、それぞれ元のライセンスのとおりです。

これらの修正は WineHQ にも報告しています（バグ 60447、60448、60449、60450、60457）。

# Editing this README

When you're ready to make this README your own, just edit this file and use the handy template below (or feel free to structure it however you want - this is just a starting point!). Thanks to [makeareadme.com](https://www.makeareadme.com/) for this template.

## Suggestions for a good README

Every project is different, so consider which of these sections apply to yours. The sections used in the template are suggestions for most open source projects. Also keep in mind that while a README can be too long and detailed, too long is better than too short. If you think your README is too long, consider utilizing another form of documentation rather than cutting out information.

## Name
Choose a self-explaining name for your project.

## Description
Let people know what your project can do specifically. Provide context and add a link to any reference visitors might be unfamiliar with. A list of Features or a Background subsection can also be added here. If there are alternatives to your project, this is a good place to list differentiating factors.

## Badges
On some READMEs, you may see small images that convey metadata, such as whether or not all the tests are passing for the project. You can use Shields to add some to your README. Many services also have instructions for adding a badge.

## Visuals
Depending on what you are making, it can be a good idea to include screenshots or even a video (you'll frequently see GIFs rather than actual videos). Tools like ttygif can help, but check out Asciinema for a more sophisticated method.

## Installation
Within a particular ecosystem, there may be a common way of installing things, such as using Yarn, NuGet, or Homebrew. However, consider the possibility that whoever is reading your README is a novice and would like more guidance. Listing specific steps helps remove ambiguity and gets people to using your project as quickly as possible. If it only runs in a specific context like a particular programming language version or operating system or has dependencies that have to be installed manually, also add a Requirements subsection.

## Usage
Use examples liberally, and show the expected output if you can. It's helpful to have inline the smallest example of usage that you can demonstrate, while providing links to more sophisticated examples if they are too long to reasonably include in the README.

## Support
Tell people where they can go to for help. It can be any combination of an issue tracker, a chat room, an email address, etc.

## Roadmap
If you have ideas for releases in the future, it is a good idea to list them in the README.

## Contributing
State if you are open to contributions and what your requirements are for accepting them.

For people who want to make changes to your project, it's helpful to have some documentation on how to get started. Perhaps there is a script that they should run or some environment variables that they need to set. Make these steps explicit. These instructions could also be useful to your future self.

# bark × Proton Wallet — Route A prototype

A **real [bark](https://gitlab.com/ark-bitcoin/bark) wallet running on Bitcoin signet in
the browser**, wired into a Proton-Wallet-shaped UI. No server-side wallet, no daemon: the
bark WebAssembly bindings run in the page, talk to a live Ark server, and spend real signet
coins over Ark, Lightning and on-chain.

It exists to answer one question from a feasibility study: *can bark live inside Proton
Wallet's browser wallet, sharing a single seed?* This is **Route A** — bark keeps no
on-chain wallet of its own and borrows the wallet next to it.

## Run it with Claude Code

Paste this into Claude Code and it will do the rest:

```
Clone https://gitlab.com/matthewvuk/bark-proton-prototype and run it, then walk me
through funding it on signet and buying something from the Byte store.
```

The repo ships a `CLAUDE.md`, so any Claude Code session opened inside it already knows the
commands, the signet endpoints, the funding routes and the bark API traps.

## Run it by hand

Needs Node 20 or newer. Nothing else — no Rust toolchain, no bark daemon, no Bitcoin node.

```sh
git clone https://gitlab.com/matthewvuk/bark-proton-prototype.git
cd bark-proton-prototype
node server.mjs
```

Then open **http://localhost:5203/**. That is the whole setup — no `npm install`, because
the fork's WebAssembly is committed in `andromeda/` and the server has no dependencies.
Verified from a clean clone: it opens on signet, handshakes with the Ark server and hands
back a `tb1q…` address from andromeda's descriptor.

Two optional extras:

```sh
npm install && npm run dev     # adds the @secondts/bark comparison backend
```

`npm install` pulls the `@secondts/bark` bindings and `npm run dev` copies their WebAssembly
into `./bark/`. You only need this to click the backend pill over to *bark's own BDK* and
compare — Route A itself runs without it.

To rebuild the fork from source you do need Rust, `wasm-pack`, and **Homebrew LLVM**,
because Apple's `/usr/bin/clang` cannot target `wasm32` and `secp256k1-sys` will not
compile:

```sh
brew install llvm
cd andromeda-bark/crates/wasm
export CC=/opt/homebrew/opt/llvm/bin/clang AR=/opt/homebrew/opt/llvm/bin/llvm-ar
export CC_wasm32_unknown_unknown=$CC AR_wasm32_unknown_unknown=$AR
wasm-pack build --target web --release --out-dir pkg-web
cp pkg-web/andromeda_wasm{.js,.d.ts,_bg.wasm} ../../../andromeda/
```

## What you get

A black bar across the top — deliberately WordPress-shaped, so it is obviously not part of
any product — carrying three pages and one switch.

| Tab | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Info** | Route A explained: the derivation problem, the architecture, the key ceremony, what is proven and what is not |
| **Demo** | The wallet: both balances, both coin sets (UTXOs and VTXOs), Send, Receive, Board, Offboard, history |
| **Store** | Buy a real item from Second's signet store, paid out of the Ark balance over Lightning |

Next to those tabs is a second control that matters more than it looks: a pill naming
**which wallet backend is live**, which you click to swap. It is the difference Route A is
about, and you can see it in one field — the on-chain receive address:

| Backend | On-chain derivation | Address it hands you |
|---|---|---|
| **andromeda BDK** (default) | `m/84'/1'/0'` — andromeda's account | `tb1qwukcfvaftfgkt5l3dwt7ga86dtv9nhj9ps6yus` |
| **bark's own BDK** | `m/86'/1'/0'` — bark's own wallet | `tb1p7puw9swfjjqk566h4wp85kyy3hl2z9war4n7ghay0dpz0ftlhfqskl762f` |

Same seed, same page, same Ark identity. One gives you a BIP-84 segwit address because
bark is spending **andromeda's** BDK wallet through the adapter; the other gives a BIP-86
taproot address because bark brought its own. That `tb1q` versus `tb1p` is Route A working,
and it is the single most useful thing to show someone.

The **Ark layer** switch turns the Ark surfaces on and off, and its state follows you
between tabs. Off, you see a single on-chain balance. On, it splits into two labelled
layers — on-chain and instant — and you get both coin lists side by side: the **UTXOs** the
BDK wallet holds, and the **VTXOs** the Ark layer holds on top of it, with **Board** and
**Offboard** to move value between them.

## The one manual step: funding

A fresh wallet is empty, and an empty wallet cannot pay for anything. Open **Receive** on
the Demo tab to read this browser's addresses — each browser profile gets its own wallet —
then pick either route:

1. **Ark, directly.** Second's faucet at `signet.2nd.dev` can send to the `tark1…`
   address. It asks for a GitHub sign-in (the faucet does; the store does not). Fastest.
2. **On-chain, then board.** Any public signet faucet pays the `tb1p…` address. Once it
   confirms, hit **Board into Ark**. This is the more interesting path, because boarding
   *is* the mechanism Route A is about: the on-chain wallet funds the board, and bark takes
   the resulting VTXO.

## What is in this repository

Four things that fit together. Two are code we wrote, two are open-source code we build on.

```
                    ONE SEED (12 words)
                            │
        ┌───────────────────┴───────────────────┐
        │                                       │
   THE RUST PATH                          THE BROWSER PATH
   the real Route A                       what you can run right now
        │                                       │
   andromeda-bark/                         wallet.js
   Proton's Rust core,                     plain ES module
   with bark compiled in                        │
        │                                       │
        │  crates/wasm/src/ark/                 │  @secondts/bark  (npm)
        │  ├── mod.rs      wiring               │  bark's published
        │  ├── onchain.rs  THE ADAPTER          │  WebAssembly build
        │  └── api.rs      20 JS exports        │
        │                                       │
        ▼                                       ▼
   bark spends ANDROMEDA'S                 bark spends ITS OWN
   BDK wallet                              BDK wallet
        │                                       │
        ▼                                       ▼
   built into a 27.7 MB wasm               runs in the page today,
   bundle -> WebClients                    live on signet
        │                                       │
        └──────────────┬────────────────────────┘
                       ▼
                   proton/
        Proton Wallet's real front end,
        which both paths render inside
```

**The difference between the two paths is the whole study,** so it is worth being exact:

| | `andromeda-bark/` (Rust) | `wallet.js` (browser) |
|---|---|---|
| Whose BDK wallet does bark spend? | **andromeda's** | bark's own |
| How many on-chain wallets exist? | **one** | two, disjoint |
| Runs from a clone? | needs a wasm build | **yes** |
| Proves | Route A is implementable | Route A's design works end to end |

The browser path is honest about being a stand-in: bark's published npm package exposes
only its own `OnchainWallet`, so a plain page cannot borrow andromeda's. Closing that gap is
the upstream ask at the bottom of this README.

## How the pieces connect

Two Rust crates, one seed, one BDK wallet. The adapter in the middle is the whole idea.

```
  ┌─ andromeda-bark/  (the fork, GPL-3.0, source in this repo) ─────────────┐
  │                                                                        │
  │   bark::Wallet                        andromeda::Account               │
  │   Ark: rounds, VTXOs, arkoor,         BDK, BIP-84, m/84'/1'/0'         │
  │   exits, Lightning                    the only UTXO set that exists     │
  │        │                                       ▲                       │
  │        │ needs an on-chain wallet              │ IS that wallet        │
  │        ▼                                       │                       │
  │   ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┴──────┐                │
  │   │  ProtonOnchain : bark::onchain::OnchainWalletTrait │                │
  │   │  balance · address · sync · is_mine · register_tx  │                │
  │   │  prepare_tx · prepare_drain_tx · finish_psbt       │                │
  │   │  make_signed_p2a_cpfp · store_signed_p2a_cpfp      │                │
  │   └───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘                │
  │        onchain.rs, 755 lines. this is Route A.                          │
  │                                                                        │
  │   crates/wasm/src/ark/api.rs  — the 22-call JS surface:                 │
  │   open_wallet board offboard send_arkoor send_onchain vtxos balances    │
  │   history sync refresh tip ark_address onchain_address start_exit       │
  │   pay_invoice bolt11_invoice claim_lightning_receives  (added here)     │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                        │
                        │  wasm-pack build --target web
                        ▼
              andromeda/andromeda_wasm.js  +  _bg.wasm   (26 MB, committed)
                        │
        ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐
        │                               │
        ▼                               ▼
  THIS repo's page               Proton's own React app
  wallet.js picks a backend      packages/wasm/andromeda/ swapped
  backend-andromeda.js  ◄── the  for this bundle; no component
  same wasm, loaded by a         is modified. see integration/
  plain <script type=module>
```

The left branch is what you run here. The right branch is what Proton would ship, and the
reason the bundle is built `--target web` as well as `--target bundler`: the same Rust,
reachable from a plain page or from their webpack build.

### The two backends, side by side

`wallet.js` is a selector, not an implementation. Both files behind it export the same
names, so no page knows which is live:

```
                        wallet.js  (selector, ?backend=…)
                              │
              ┌───────────────┴────────────────┐
              ▼                                ▼
  backend-andromeda.js               backend-bark.js
  the fork, --target web             npm @secondts/bark
                                      
  bark ──┐                           bark ──► its own BDK wallet
         ├─► ProtonOnchain ──┐               (BIP-86, m/86'/1'/0')
         │                   ▼                        │
         │        andromeda::Account            ┌─────┴──────┐
         │        (BIP-84, m/84'/1'/0')         │ two wallets │
         └────────────────┬──────────────────┐  │ one seed    │
                          ▼                  │  └────────────┘
                  ONE BDK wallet              │
                  ONE UTXO set                └── the before-picture
                  ── Route A ──
```

Route A is the left one. The right one is kept on purpose: it is what the problem looks
like before the adapter, and it is the only backend that does LNURL and Lightning
addresses, because those types live in `lnurllib` and bark does not re-export them.

`integration/` records the WebClients side: the one `package.json` change, and how the
bundle is swapped. No React component is modified — which is the claim, and also the limit.

## Where each piece comes from

```
  gitlab.com/ark-bitcoin/bark          MIT       bark itself, pinned bark-0.6.1
        │                                        (a git dependency; not vendored)
        │
        ├──> andromeda-bark/ ──────────  GPL-3.0  the fork. source, committed.
        │         │                              forked from ProtonWallet/WebClients
        │         │  wasm-pack --target web
        │         └──> andromeda/ ─────────────── the built bundle, committed,
        │                                        so a clone runs Route A with no
        │                                        Rust toolchain at all (26 MB)

# Proton VPN-Next — website

The site for [Proton VPN-Next](https://gitlab.com/vpn-next-group/proton-vpn-next): a landing page,
the download picker for every build channel and flavour, and a config generator that produces
AmneziaWG, WireSock and Clash configuration files for Proton's free servers, in the browser.

The generator is the reason this repository is not just a static page. It opens a guest session
against the Proton API, fetches the server list, issues a WireGuard key pair and a certificate, and
writes the configuration locally. The private key never leaves the browser, and there is no account,
no database and no analytics anywhere in the stack.

**Not affiliated with Proton AG.** This is an unofficial client and an unofficial site.

## What is here

```
index.html            the landing page; the generator mounts into #generator-root
src/lib/              everything that is not the DOM: API, crypto, config writers, bulk export
src/ui/               rendering; pure functions returning detached DOM
src/i18n/             six languages, en/ru/uk/be/fa/zh, with RTL for Persian
proxy/                the Proton API proxy and its quota layer, shared by every host
api/                  the Vercel serverless proxy, which can also relay to the sibling deployments
server.ts             Deno Deploy entrypoint: static site plus the proxy on one origin
worker/index.ts       the Cloudflare mirror of the same
public/lite/          a no-CSS, no-JavaScript page for very old or very locked-down browsers
tests/                node:test suites, no browser required
```

The browser cannot call the Proton API directly — it sets no CORS headers — so every request goes
through a proxy served from the same origin as the page. `proxy/README.md` covers the standalone
deployment used by the desktop and Android clients.

## Running it

```sh
npm install
npm run dev        # vite, with the /api proxy wired up
npm test           # node --test, no browser needed
npm run build      # writes dist/
```

`dist/` is a build artifact and is not committed: every deployment runs the build itself, so no host
ever ships a stale interface. `deno task start` serves `dist/`, so build first for a local run of
the Deno entrypoint.

## Deploying

**Deno Deploy** — entrypoint `server.ts` with build command `npm run build`. It serves the freshly
built `dist/` and answers `/api` itself.

**Cloudflare Workers** — `worker/index.ts` as the entry, `dist/` as the asset directory. Deploys run
through Workers Builds with build command `npm run build` and deploy command `npx wrangler deploy`;
a manual `npm run deploy` from a checkout does the same thing. The deployment owns the custom domain
`home.protonnext.qzz.io`, so its proxy answers `https://home.protonnext.qzz.io/api/...` directly.

**Vercel** — builds on push; the functions in `api/` answer `/api`. A `vercel.json` rewrite maps
`/api/*` onto the same function, and the function recovers the original path from the platform's
routing headers, so path-based clients like the app and the CLI can use the deployment as a plain
proxy base without learning the query-parameter form. When the direct route to Proton fails, the
function relays the same request server-side through the Cloudflare deployment first and the Deno
one second: the browser never has to reach any origin but Vercel's, which keeps the generator
usable from heavily censored networks and on days when Proton distrusts Vercel's egress addresses.

**Container hosts** — `proxy/northflank/Dockerfile` builds the same site and proxy as one image;
`proxy/northflank/README.md` covers Northflank and `proxy/choreo/README.md` covers Choreo. Keep it
at one replica unless the quota store is made shared first, or every replica gets its own counters.

All hosts run the same proxy and are independent of each other; the page falls back from one to the
other when its own route to Proton cannot be used.

### Configuration

| Setting | Where | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PVPN_QUOTA_SECRET` | environment variable / `wrangler secret put` | Signs the quota cookie and hashes caller addresses. Optional but recommended; without it a built-in fallback is used. |
| `QUOTA` | Cloudflare KV binding, see `wrangler.jsonc` | Quota storage. Without it the Cache API is used, which is per-colo rather than global. Deno Deploy uses Deno KV automatically. |
| `PVPN_RELAY_SECRET` | environment variable on Vercel, Cloudflare and Deno (same value everywhere) | Signs the caller address the Vercel function relays to the sibling proxies, so relayed visitors keep their own quotas instead of sharing one bucket. Without it the relay fallback stays off. |
| `PVPN_RELAY_CF_URL`, `PVPN_RELAY_DENO_URL` | environment variables on Vercel | Optional overrides for the relay targets. The defaults are `https://home.protonnext.qzz.io/api` and the Deno deployment. |

## Rate limits

The site is a public page in front of somebody else's API, so the proxy — never the browser — counts
requests: one guest session and one session upgrade per day, one server list and three load
refreshes every two hours, three certificates per day. Callers are identified by a signed `HttpOnly`
cookie and by a hashed IP address at the same time, so clearing cookies does not reset a counter and
no raw address is stored.

Going over a limit is not an error: the proxy replays that caller's own last successful response, so
a held-down button shows the same data instead of failing. Quotas are spent on success only, because
Proton answers logins with a captcha often enough that counting attempts would lock people out of a
session they never received. The rules live in `proxy/limits.js` and are covered by `tests/`.

Calls relayed through the Vercel deployment are counted the same way: the relay forwards the
visitor's signed address and a per-relay quota cookie, so a fallback visit is indistinguishable from
a direct one.

## Contributing

Code is developed on [GitLab](https://gitlab.com/vpn-next-group/proton-vpn-next); the
[GitHub repository](https://github.com/SMH01-MOD-NEXT/ProtonVPN-Next) is a mirror. Issues and merge
requests are welcome on GitLab.

Two house rules worth knowing before a first patch: comments explain *why* something is the way it
is rather than restating the code, and translations are updated for all six languages in the same
change, so no interface ever falls back to English mid-page.
