https://gitlab.com/renat.kravchenko/aero.description:
Aerolink is a companion gateway between a PX4 vehicle and the operator's phone. It mirrors live state — armed, flight mode, battery, satellites, altitude, mission, fleet position — onto a paired Android device, while QGroundControl keeps flying the aircraft.

It is deliberately not a GCS. The desktop gateway listens on the companion port 14540, never on QGC's 14550, and identifies itself with system id 253, so it never competes for the vehicle: it reads state and sends no commands. The phone never speaks MAVLink to the aircraft at all — only to the desktop, in a private dialect (420).

• Pairing is a handshake, not a shared password: ephemeral X25519 plus PBKDF2/HKDF over an XXXX-XXXX code, with per-direction session keys that die with the session — forward secrecy the earlier fixed-key scheme never had.
• Every frame travels in an ALK3 envelope: AES-256-GCM, counter nonces, a sliding replay window, and a 30-second freshness check against a clock offset learned during the handshake, so two devices that have never seen NTP still link.
• The carrier is a seam, not an assumption: UDP over Wi-Fi and TCP serve the same port 41234 at once, and the phone picks one per desktop it finds. USB-serial over OTG and BLE are the seam's reason for existing.
• One channel, many aircraft: vehicles arrive on a single link and are told apart by MAVLink system id, each with its own status, track, mission cache and staleness clock. A vehicle that goes quiet stays visible for twenty seconds, faded and marked lost.
• Two map renderers over one shared model: a ~400-line slippy-map renderer on a Compose Canvas over raster tiles (desktop) and MapLibre over OpenFreeMap vector styles (phone). Colour wheel, marker shape, follow logic and mission state machine are shared; only the surface differs. No API keys anywhere.

Stack: Kotlin Multiplatform, Compose Multiplatform, Android client and Desktop JVM gateway.

# Aerolink Aerolink is a **companion gateway**: it mirrors a drone's live state — armed, flight mode, battery, satellites, altitude — onto a paired phone over an encrypted private link, while QGroundControl keeps flying the aircraft. ![Aerolink in use: the phone mirrored over the gateway's own map, QGroundControl's vehicle rail down the right, one fleet of four moving on all three at once — and a vehicle's card opening on the phone at the end](media/demo.gif) ![Aerolink Desktop: four vehicles under way, each with its own mission drawn in its own colour](media/desktop_map_fleet.jpg) ## Why this is not a GCS PX4 sends its telemetry to QGroundControl on UDP **14550**; Aerolink Desktop never binds that port — it listens on **14540**, the companion/offboard port, and identifies itself as a GCS with **system id 253** so it never competes with QGC for the vehicle. Nothing here sends `COMMAND_LONG`, uploads a mission, or moves a stick: the gateway reads state and forwards a digest of it. The phone never speaks MAVLink to the aircraft at all — it only ever talks to the desktop, in a private dialect sealed with session keys a pairing handshake produced. ```mermaid flowchart LR PX4["PX4 / SITL
autopilot"] QGC["QGroundControl
GCS — flies the aircraft"] DESK["Aerolink Desktop
companion gateway"] PHONE["Aerolink Android
status screen"] PX4 -- "common MAVLink · UDP 14550" --> QGC PX4 -- "common MAVLink · UDP 14540" --> DESK DESK -. "GCS HEARTBEAT · sysid 253" .-> PX4 PHONE <-- "dialect 420 + AES-256-GCM · Wi-Fi or TCP · 41234" --> DESK ``` The two channels are deliberately different. The flight channel is plain unsigned MAVLink. The operator channel is a private dialect with AES-256-GCM and a pairing code. ## The operator link The phone pairs with the desktop by typing the `XXXX-XXXX` code the desktop shows. That code is not a shared password but the input to a handshake: a recording of it reveals nothing about the code, and the session keys it produces die with the session, so traffic recorded today cannot be opened tomorrow. The link runs over Wi-Fi or TCP, and the phone finds the desktop on either by itself. ![The gateway screen: the pairing code a phone has to match, the marks that show it as a QR or replace it, the address the gateway answers on, and the phone that got through](media/desktop_pairing.png) How the handshake, the keys and the carriers work: [docs/operator-link.md](docs/operator-link.md). ## The map Both apps draw the whole fleet on a map — every aircraft in its own colour, with its track and its mission. The desktop renders its own raster map so the vehicles and the ground share one surface; the phone uses a vector map that turns and zooms the way every other map on a phone does. No API keys anywhere. On the desktop the map can also take a window of its own, to be thrown onto a projector or a second monitor. That window is for watching rather than clicking: it shows the fleet, how far along its mission each aircraft is, and nothing that reaches into it. ![The second window on its own screen: the same fleet, the status line and the chips as a legend, the routes switch and full screen — and none of the actions that reach into the fleet](media/desktop_second_screen_map.jpg) More: [docs/map.md](docs/map.md). ## The fleet One link, many aircraft. Both apps carry a **Борти** tab with one card per vehicle — battery, altitude and speed set large enough to read at a glance — and picking a card is the same choice as picking a vehicle on the map. An aircraft that goes quiet stays on screen, faded and marked lost, so a dropout is something the operator sees rather than infers. Every change to a vehicle's route is kept, and earlier versions can be laid over the map. ![The same tab on the desktop: four cards, the same colours, the same monospaced battery, altitude and speed the phone draws](media/desktop_uav.png) More: [docs/fleet.md](docs/fleet.md). ## The black box The desktop records every frame the aircraft send, exactly as they arrived. A recorded flight opens on the same map the live screen uses, with a scale to move through it and the moments worth jumping to — takeoffs, landings, a low battery, a lost fix — marked along it; each aircraft gets a summary of its flight. A flight also leaves as a `.tlog` that QGroundControl opens, or as a track in GeoJSON or CSV. ![A flight opened from the black box: the same tracks, chips and colours the live map draws, the scale under it with the flight's events marked along it, and beside it what one aircraft did over the whole flight](media/desktop_history_map.jpg) More: [docs/black-box.md](docs/black-box.md). ## Video and object detection The desktop shows each aircraft's camera — in a window of its own, or the whole fleet in one window, as a grid or as one main picture beside the rest. A vehicle with a fault is framed in the alert colour there, so trouble is visible without a look at the map. Video stays on the desktop; the phone never receives a frame. ![The window with every vehicle's video: one main picture and the rest in a column beside it, the detector's boxes over all three](media/desktop_video_wall.jpg) Over the video the desktop can mark what is on it — people in amber, vehicles in cyan — with a YOLO model the operator points it at. One detector serves the whole fleet, and a box that has fallen behind the picture is not drawn, because it would mark where something was rather than where it is. ![One vehicle's window: people in amber, cars and vans in cyan, each with its class and confidence](media/desktop_video_detect.jpg) More: [docs/video.md](docs/video.md). ## Further reading * [docs/](docs/README.md) — how each part works and why: the link, the map, the fleet, the black box, video. * [docs/running.md](docs/running.md) — building and running, PX4 SITL, the bench scripts. * [`ARCHITECTURE.md`](./ARCHITECTURE.md) — module boundaries and the seams between them (Ukrainian).

https://gitlab.com/hadleen/candid-pdf-ta.description:
CandidPDFTable is a lightweight PHP library for building complex tables in TCPDF with precision and predictability.

Unlike traditional TCPDF table helpers that rely on implicit or shared borders, CandidPDFTable uses a cell-centric model where each cell explicitly owns its borders and layout rules. Column widths and colspan resolution are computed only at render time, ensuring deterministic output even in dynamic, programmatic scenarios.

Key characteristics:

* Deterministic, colspan-aware table layout
* Explicit per-cell border control (no table-level magic)
* Optional serial number column with automatic suppression for totals
* Percent-based column widths with rounding correction
* Multi-line cell content using TCPDF-compatible HTML
* Designed specifically for TCPDF::writeHTML()

This library is ideal for invoices, reports, statements, and structured PDF documents where layout correctness and reproducibility matter.

# CandidPDFTable (Candid PDF Table Builder) Deterministic, colspan-aware table builder for **TCPDF**. `candid-pdf-table` provides a clean, predictable API to construct HTML tables for `TCPDF::writeHTML()` using explicit, cell-owned borders and late layout computation. This library is designed for **programmatic table generation** where precise control over rows, columns, colspans, borders, and serial numbering is required. --- ## Why this library? Building complex tables in TCPDF is difficult once HTML is rendered. This library solves that by: - Using a **cell-centric model** (each cell owns its borders & style) - Supporting **colspan-aware addressing** - Avoiding implicit or shared borders - Computing widths and layout **only at render time** - Keeping behavior deterministic and predictable --- ## Features - Explicit, per-cell border control - Optional **serial number column** - Colspan-aware cell lookup - Header, item, row, and total rows - Percent-based column widths - Multi-line cell content via HTML - Designed specifically for TCPDF --- ## Requirements - PHP **7.4+** - **TCPDF** (must be available at runtime) --- ## Installation ```bash composer require hadleen/candid-pdf-table ``` --- ## Basic Usage ```php use Hadleen\TCPDF\Table\CandidPDFTable; $pdf = new TCPDF(); $pdf->AddPage(); $table = new CandidPDFTable(3); $table->showSerialNumber('S.NO', 8); $table->addHeaderRow(['Item','Qty','Amount']); $table->addItem(['Pen','2','20.00']); $table->addItem(['Notebook','1','50.00']); $table->addTotalRow('Total', 70.00); $table->addTableBorder(); $table->render($pdf); ``` --- ## Serial Column Enable serial numbering: ```php $table->showSerialNumber('S.NO', 8); ``` - Serial column index = `-1` - Serial numbers appear only on item rows - Header shows caption - Total rows suppress serial values --- ## Multi-line Cell Content Use HTML tags such as `
`: ```php $table->getCellAt(2,1)->setText( 'Laptop
Intel i7
16GB RAM' ); ``` > Newline characters (`\n`) are ignored by TCPDF. --- ## Borders ```php $table->showLine(2,1,'bottom'); $table->setRowLines(1,'all',1); $table->setColumnLines(-1,'left',1); $table->setColumnLines(2,'right',1); $table->addTableBorder(); $table->addOuterBorder(); $table->addInnerBorder(); ``` --- ## Column Widths ```php $table->setColumnWidth(0,60); $table->setColumnWidth(1,20); $table->setColumnWidth(2,20); ``` --- ## Cell Addressing - Rows: 1-based - Data columns: 0-based - Serial column: -1 ```php $table->getCellAt(2,0); $table->getCellAt(2,-1); ``` --- ## Render Lifecycle Layout is resolved only during `render()`. --- ## Versioning Semantic Versioning is used. Current version: **v1.0.0** --- ## License MIT License © 2026 Hadleen — Tamil Amuthan

# Editing this README

When you're ready to make this README your own, just edit this file and use the handy template below (or feel free to structure it however you want - this is just a starting point!). Thanks to [makeareadme.com](https://www.makeareadme.com/) for this template.

## Suggestions for a good README

Every project is different, so consider which of these sections apply to yours. The sections used in the template are suggestions for most open source projects. Also keep in mind that while a README can be too long and detailed, too long is better than too short. If you think your README is too long, consider utilizing another form of documentation rather than cutting out information.

## Name
Choose a self-explaining name for your project.

## Description
Let people know what your project can do specifically. Provide context and add a link to any reference visitors might be unfamiliar with. A list of Features or a Background subsection can also be added here. If there are alternatives to your project, this is a good place to list differentiating factors.

## Badges
On some READMEs, you may see small images that convey metadata, such as whether or not all the tests are passing for the project. You can use Shields to add some to your README. Many services also have instructions for adding a badge.

## Visuals
Depending on what you are making, it can be a good idea to include screenshots or even a video (you'll frequently see GIFs rather than actual videos). Tools like ttygif can help, but check out Asciinema for a more sophisticated method.

## Installation
Within a particular ecosystem, there may be a common way of installing things, such as using Yarn, NuGet, or Homebrew. However, consider the possibility that whoever is reading your README is a novice and would like more guidance. Listing specific steps helps remove ambiguity and gets people to using your project as quickly as possible. If it only runs in a specific context like a particular programming language version or operating system or has dependencies that have to be installed manually, also add a Requirements subsection.

## Usage
Use examples liberally, and show the expected output if you can. It's helpful to have inline the smallest example of usage that you can demonstrate, while providing links to more sophisticated examples if they are too long to reasonably include in the README.

## Support
Tell people where they can go to for help. It can be any combination of an issue tracker, a chat room, an email address, etc.

## Roadmap
If you have ideas for releases in the future, it is a good idea to list them in the README.

## Contributing
State if you are open to contributions and what your requirements are for accepting them.

For people who want to make changes to your project, it's helpful to have some documentation on how to get started. Perhaps there is a script that they should run or some environment variables that they need to set. Make these steps explicit. These instructions could also be useful to your future self.

You can also document commands to lint the code or run tests. These steps help to ensure high code quality and reduce the likelihood that the changes inadvertently break something. Having instructions for running tests is especially helpful if it requires external setup, such as starting a Selenium server for testing in a browser.

## Authors and acknowledgment
Show your appreciation to those who have contributed to the project.

## License
For open source projects, say how it is licensed.

## Project status
If you have run out of energy or time for your project, put a note at the top of the README saying that development has slowed down or stopped completely. Someone may choose to fork your project or volunteer to step in as a maintainer or owner, allowing your project to keep going. You can also make an explicit request for maintainers.

# Modelica_DeviceDrivers
Free library for interfacing hardware drivers to Modelica models.
There is support for joysticks, keyboards, UDP, TCP/IP, LCM, MQTT, shared memory, AD/DA converters, serial port and other devices.

## Library description
The `Modelica_DeviceDrivers` (MDD) library is an open source Modelica package that interfaces hardware drivers to Modelica models. An overview of the library is provided in

> Bernhard Thiele, Thomas Beutlich, Volker Waurich, Martin Sjölund, and Tobias Bellmann, Towards a Standard-Conform, Platform-Generic and Feature-Rich Modelica Device Drivers Library. In Jiří Kofránek and Francesco Casella, editors, _12th Int. Modelica Conference_, Prague, Czech Republic, May 2017. [Download](https://www.modelica.org/events/modelica2017/proceedings/html/submissions/ecp17132713_ThieleBeutlichWaurichSjolundBellmann.pdf)

The library unifies previous developments concerning device driver support in Modelica, see [Interactive Simulations and advanced Visualization with Modelica](https://modelica.org/events/modelica2009/Proceedings/memorystick/pages/papers/0056/0056.pdf) and [Modelica for Embedded Systems](https://modelica.org/events/modelica2009/Proceedings/memorystick/pages/papers/0096/0096.pdf) (Modelica'2009 conference). The functionality covered by this library has been used internally at DLR for several years, such as for Driver-in-the-Loop simulation and for the [DLR Robot Motion Simulator](http://www.dlr.de/media/en/desktopdefault.aspx/tabid-4995/8426_read-17606/).
The previously fragmented functionality was streamlined, improved, and extended to a coherent cross-platform library.

Main features:
  * Cross-platform (Windows and Linux).
  * (Soft) real-time synchronization of a simulation.
  * Support for keyboard, joystick/gamepad, and 3Dconnexion Spacemouse.
  * Support for a universal packaging concept to pack Modelica variables in a graphical and convenient way into a bit vector and transport such a bit vector via UDP, TCP/IP, LCM, MQTT, serial I/O or shared memory (CAN support is prototypical available).
  * Support of the Linux control and measurement device interface for digital and analog I/O (Comedi interface).

All device drivers are made available via external Modelica functions. Furthermore, high level interfaces on these functions are provided via Modelica blocks. The first interface uses Modelica 3.2 functionality only (when-clauses and sample-operator).
The second interface uses the synchronous language elements introduced in Modelica 3.3 and is based on clocks (works together with the `Modelica_Synchronous` library).

![BlockOverview](screenshot.png)

### Self-certification
 - [X] Internationalized
 - [ ] Unit tests
 - [X] End-user documentation
 - [X] Internal documentation (documentation, interfaces, etc.)
 - [X] Existed and maintained for at least 6 months

## Build status
[![Build Status](https://travis-ci.org/modelica/Modelica_DeviceDrivers.svg)](https://travis-ci.org/modelica/Modelica_DeviceDrivers)

## Current release

Download [Modelica_DeviceDrivers latest release](../../releases/latest)

Please note that the library is known to work with
* Dymola,
* SimulationX (with `userBufferSize` all non-clocked communication blocks are working in SimulationX, but `autoBufferSize` only works for external solvers CVode and Fixed Step solver and fails for BDF and MEBDF solvers, see [#54 (comment)](https://github.com/modelica/Modelica_DeviceDrivers/issues/54#issuecomment-76032325)),
* OpenModelica (partial support starting with OpenModelica v1.11.0 Beta 1, e.g., UDP, serial port, shared memory, LCM, keyboard).

If you tested the library successfully with another Modelica tool, please contact [Bernhard Thiele](https://github.com/bernhard-thiele) or send a [pull request](https://github.com/modelica/Modelica_DeviceDrivers/pulls) that updates this README.md.

#### Release notes
Bug fix releases usually won't have release notes, so please use the download link from above to get the latest release including bug fixes.

*  [Version v1.6.0 (2018-10-06)](../../releases/tag/v1.6.0)
   * Support for MQTT (Message Queuing Telemetry Transport protocol) client communication (see #130, #256).
   * Utility function to retrieve MAC address (`Utilities.Functions.getMACAddress`, see #255).
   * Utility function to generate a UUID (`Utilities.Functions.generateUUID()`, see #244).
   * Number of received bytes in `UDPReceive` block is provided as output (see #236).
   * Scalable real-time synchronization (see #215).

https://gitlab.com/atomjump/medimageserv.readme_excerpt: # MedImage Server The MedImage Server is a companion product to the MedImage apps on smart-phones. See http://medimage.co.nz The combined product enables the medical practitioner to take a photo of a patient with their mobile phone, and have the image transferred directly into a specific folder on their PC or server. The image is tagged with a patient id immediately before the photo is taken. The most common way to install this package is to use an internet connected PC as a 'proxy' (typically linux based), which temporarily holds the photos that are uploaded from the phone via 3G/4G to the server. A Windows Med Image reader sits on the Doctor's PC, which reads the proxy on a regular basis, and downloads images directly into a chosen folder (or folders) on the PC ## 1. To Install Your Proxy This is useful when you cannot have a Wifi connection, and must go via a secure internet connection. On a linux based server, first install NodeJS and npm. See https://www.digitalocean.com/community/tutorials/how-to-install-node-js-on-an-ubuntu-14-04-server Then: ``` eval "$(curl -fsSL -H 'Cache-Control: no-cache' https://git.atomjump.com/medimageserv-linstaller.git/install)" ``` (Or for a super user installation, which is sometimes required) ``` eval "$(curl -fsSL -H 'Cache-Control: no-cache' https://git.atomjump.com/medimageserv-linstaller.git/install-root)" ``` Alternatively, if these do not match your server's permissions, you can find the list of individual commands at https://git.atomjump.com/medimageserv-linstaller.git/install https://git.atomjump.com/medimageserv-linstaller.git/install-root Run the command the last part of the script displays, to get autostart at boot-up. You may have to open the firewall to port 5566 for reading and writing eg.: ``` sudo ufw allow 5566/tcp ``` To start MedImage server ``` pm2 start medimage-server ``` To stop MedImage server: ``` pm2 stop medimage-server ``` To restart (after any config.json changes): ``` pm2 restart medimage-server ``` For logging or and any permissions issues, see the section 'Troubleshooting' below. Note: this proxy daemon is always on, but the images are only kept on this machine for a few seconds. ## 2. On your Windows PC/local server Download and run the installable MedImageServer.exe from http://medimage.co.nz If you have installed your own proxy using npm, above, enter the URL of your proxy server eg. 'https://myproxy.mycompany.com:5566' into the third large button. You will be given a 4 digit pairing code. ## 3. On your MedImage Android/iPhone app Search the Play Store or App store for 'MedImage'. Purchase and install. Click the large blue/purple button on the app to connect and start taking photos. If you have no wifi connection it will ask you for your 4 character pairing code from your server. Enter the patient id in the box at the top, specific to each photo. Note: #tags will allocate a directory (this will create another subdirectory inside your directory.). eg. ``` #elderly Fred ``` would create a directory called elderly/ on your PC and upload a file called 'Fred-[datetime]' ## Options These are located in the file config.json. * **backupTo** should be an array of linux-style paths where the files are backed up to. * **readProxy** should be null if this is the master 'proxy' server, but will be set automatically after you sync. * **listenPort** is the port on your server which is open to being read * **httpsKey** is optional. If you are on an https server, it is required (an http server should leave this blank). It is a file path to the key .pem file which includes your private ssl key. * **httpsCert** is optional. If you are on an https server, it is required (an http server should leave this blank). It is a file path to the certificate .pem file which includes your server's ssl certificate. * **onStartBackupDriveDetect** is optional. If set to 'true' it autodetects new drives added when starting, and will backup your new photos to: New Drive:\MedImage\photos * **allowPhotosLeaving** If set to 'true', this allows photos to leave the machine and be downloaded by other installations of the server. Leave 'true' for proxy servers, but false for client Windows machines. * **allowGettingRemotePhotos** If set to 'true', this allows photos to be downloaded from a remote proxy server. If this is a proxy server, this should be set to 'false', otherwise for client Windows machines, set to 'true'. * **webProxy** If your web browser usually requires a proxy server (i.e. for normal web requests), then use the option"webProxy", in this format: "http://yourUser:yourPassword@webProxyIPaddress:webProxyPort" * **lockDown** You can switch a server into 'lock down' mode, where the interface cannot change any settings, add-ons, or see any technical logs, by setting this to 'true'. Ver >= 1.3.6 * **basicAuthent** Enter a human readable password for addons that need some light security. This is a global password visible only within the config file (anyone with file level access to the server can see this). Ver >= 1.3.8 * **allowedTypes** Provide the ability to upload additional file types other than basic .jpg photos, e.g. PDF. You need to specify the extension and the MIME type in a new array element e.g. { "extension": ".pdf", "mime": "application/pdf" } ## Troubleshooting Once the server is running, you can check the logs with ``` pm2 logs ``` Note: the permissions and ownership of the following files/directories may need to be expanded (try with 'chmod 777' at first, and then restrict the permissions once this is working). ``` /usr/lib/node_modules/medimage/config.json # must be writable by the sudo node script /usr/lib/node_modules/medimage/photos ``` ``` chmod 777 config.json chown nobody:ubuntu config.json # nobody:ubuntu will vary slightly depending on platform chmod 777 photos chown nobody:ubuntu photos ``` If you are having problems installing the medimage software on a small machine (e.g. with 512MB RAM), please try ``` sudo npm install -g medimage -production ``` ## Upgrade script The way to upgrade Medimage Server: ``` eval "$(curl -fsSL -H 'Cache-Control: no-cache' https://git.atomjump.com/medimageserv-linstaller.git/upgrade)" ``` But, please note, that any files in the lib/node_modules/medimage/ directory may be removed, during the 'npm install' command. If you store any other files such as keys, ensure you copy them out before running this command. (Or for a super user installation, which is sometimes required) ``` eval "$(curl -fsSL -H 'Cache-Control: no-cache' https://git.atomjump.com/medimageserv-linstaller.git/upgrade-root)" ``` You also may wish to save your config file somewhere else first, and then run: ``` npm config set medimage:configFile /path/to/your/medimage/config.json ``` Your settings will be kept between upgrades, provided the config.json is out of your global medimage directory, without having to copy them out. ## Uninstall script To remove any instances of MedImage Server: ``` eval "$(curl -fsSL -H 'Cache-Control: no-cache' https://git.atomjump.com/medimageserv-linstaller.git/uninstall)" ``` ## Getting the latest CA certificates This is needed on some machines to ensure there are no errors when requesting from the pairing server. Before building a binary with the module ssl-root-cas, change the file node_modules/ssl-root-cas/ca-store-generator.js CERTDB_URL value to: ``` https://hg.mozilla.org/projects/nss/raw-file/tip/lib/ckfw/builtins/certdata.txt ``` To refresh the list of root CAs, delete the file (on e.g. Windows) ``` C:\MedImage\node_modules\ssl-root-cas\ssl-root-cas-latest.js ``` Then restart the server (or Windows Service) twice. The file above should be regenerated with the latest CA records. ## Photo and folder drainage This will keep your system running optimally: ``` sudo crontab -e ``` or ``` crontab -e ``` and add the lines (replacing '/path/to/node' with your own node path) : ``` # Daily removal of empty practice and nhid folders 0 0 * * * /usr/bin/find /path/to/node/node_modules/medimage/photos/. -empty -type d -delete # Weekly removal of 6 month old photos and messages 0 0 * * 0 /usr/bin/find /path/to/node/node_modules/medimage/photos -type f -name '*.jpg' -mtime +182 -exec rm {} \; 0 0 * * 0 /usr/bin/find /path/to/node/node_modules/medimage/photos -type f -name '*.json' -mtime +182 -exec rm {} \; ``` Note: you will need to do something similar on Windows, though we don't have instructions for this platform yet. # License Application source code copyright (c) 2018 AtomJump Ltd. You may obtain a copy of the License at http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0 Unless required by applicable law or agreed to in writing, software distributed under the License is distributed on an "AS IS" BASIS, WITHOUT WARRANTIES OR CONDITIONS OF ANY KIND, either express or implied. https://gitlab.com/nerdocs/thrito/thrito.readme_excerpt:
# thrito-austria

The Austrian core: the patient's SVNR (`PatientAT`), the payers' Kassencodes (`InsuranceAT`), the e-card treatment
cases and the e-card system itself — workstation login, card reads, consultations. What Austria adds to
prescribing lives in `thrito-austria-medication`, what it adds to the settlement in `thrito-austria-billing`; both
depend on this package, never the other way round, so a practice without a medication or billing module still
installs the e-card. See `docs/`.

## General

Thrito modules are living in the `thrito.plugins` setuptools entrypoint group.
They are normal Django apps, but found and loaded dynamically during startup when installed via pip.
As Django apps, they can have everything a "static" app also has:

#### Austria PluginConfig

The app configuration is declared in the module's `apps.py`. Set the plugin's metadata there in the PluginMeta class.


## Install

You can install this plugin locally during development into Thrito by invoking `pip install -e .` in this folder, assuming you have activated your main project's virtualenv.

If you want to test this plugin on its own, you can also use a separate virtualenv for it:

```bash
virtualenv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e .
```

This should install Thrito austria editable in the virtual environment.

## Testing

Testing is done using pytest. Just call it in the root dir:
```
pytest
```

## Models

Create your models as usual in `models.py`, they will be included. Don't forget to run `makemigrations` and `migrate` afterwords.


After each change regarding version number etc., run `python manage.py syncplugins`. This ensures your database is in sync with the plugins on disk.

## License

This plugin is licensed under the [GNU Affero General Public License v3 or later (AGPLv3+)](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/agpl-3.0.txt)

[build-system]
requires = ["setuptools >= 78.0", "cython >= 0.29.0"]
build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

[project]
name = "thrito-austria"
dynamic = ["version"]
description = "Austria core: SVNR, the payers' Kassencodes and the e-card system (login, card reads, consultations)."
readme = "README.md"
license = { file = "LICENSE.md" }
authors = [
    { name = "Christian González", email = "christian.gonzalez@nerdocs.at" },
]
requires-python = ">=3.13"
classifiers = [
    "License :: OSI Approved :: GNU Affero General Public License v3 or later (AGPLv3+)",
]
# The Austrian core. What Austria adds to prescribing is thrito-austria-medication,
# what it adds to the settlement thrito-austria-billing — both depend on this
# package, never the other way round.
dependencies = [
    "django>=6.0.4",
    "thrito",
    "thrito-patients",  # Patient master data: models, interfaces, signals
    "thrito-emr-import",  # SVNR matcher for foreign-EMR imports
    "ecard[soap]",  # e-card client library (../ecard); [soap] = zeep/lxml SOAP transport (AUTH/SAS/VDAS), required at runtime
    "elga",  # ELGA CDA + the EMS physician notification (../elga)
]

#[project.urls]
#Source = "https://gitlab.com/..."
#Tracker = "https://gitlab.com/.../issues"

[project.entry-points."thrito.plugins"]
austria = "thrito.plugins.austria:apps.AustriaConfig"

[dependency-groups]
dev = [
    "pytest>=7.0",
    "pytest-django",
    "pytest-playwright",
    "ecard[soap]",  # e-card SoapTransport (zeep/lxml) for dev/runtime use
]

[tool.setuptools.dynamic]
version = {attr = "thrito.plugins.austria.__version__"}

[tool.setuptools.packages.find]
where = ["src"]

[tool.setuptools.package-data]
# The Svelte bundle is gitignored build output, but it has to travel in the
# wheel: without it the installed plugin has no bundle and the GDAPS bundle
# view answers 404 for every component this plugin declares. Run
# `manage.py buildfrontend --plugin austria` before `python -m build`.
# The ``kassen-at`` bundle travels in the wheel too: an installation without a
# Thrito Hub seeds the payers and treatment cases from it (``master_data.py``).
"thrito.plugins.austria" = ["frontend/dist/*.js", "data/kassen-at.tar"]

It generates structured, HIPAA-compliant medical notes, suggests ICD-10/CPT/HCPCS/SNOMED codes, and exports to C-CDA or FHIR formats. With encrypted storage, specialty-specific templates, advanced voice commands, patient-friendly summaries, and a modern dual-pane UI, ScribeVault streamlines documentation, supports physician approval workflows, and ensures security and compliance for clinics and hospitals.  https://roxanneardary.com/scribevault/

# ScribeVault
**Encrypted, HIPAA-Compliant, AI-Driven.**
- HTML Mirror:  [https://roxanneardary.com/scribevault-specification/](https://roxanneardary.com/scribevault-specification/)  

---

ScribeVault is an open-source AI-driven clinical documentation platform designed to function as a real-time medical scribe and post-visit documentation system for hospitals, clinics, private practices, and other healthcare environments.

ScribeVault captures clinical conversations, transforms them into structured documentation, assists with medical coding, supports voice-driven workflows, maintains encrypted patient records, and provides interoperability for clinical and insurance workflows. The system is designed for fully self-hosted deployment with user-selectable storage and a modular AI architecture.

## Purpose

ScribeVault is designed to reduce the administrative burden of clinical documentation while keeping clinicians in control of the final medical record.

The system shall:

- Capture clinical conversations through real-time voice transcription
- Process uploaded recordings for post-visit documentation
- Transform conversations into structured clinical notes
- Organize information into HPI, ROS, Examination, Assessment, and Plan
- Suggest ICD-10, CPT, HCPCS, and SNOMED codes
- Provide detailed coding information for clinician review and approval
- Prepare approved documentation for insurance submission workflows
- Support medication reconciliation
- Identify and surface documented allergies
- Provide specialty-specific documentation templates
- Support voice-controlled clinical workflows
- Generate patient-facing summaries
- Record and document consent
- Provide patient education materials
- Maintain an encounter timeline
- Highlight uncertain or low-confidence information
- Export clinical documentation through interoperable formats
- Keep protected health information encrypted and under the control of the deploying organization

## Design Principles

ScribeVault shall follow these principles:

- Clinician-controlled documentation
- Human approval before clinical or billing submission
- Privacy-first architecture
- Encryption of protected health information
- Fully self-hosted operation
- User-selectable data storage
- Modular AI architecture
- Vendor-neutral integrations
- Interoperability
- Auditable clinical workflows
- Specialty-aware documentation
- Explainable AI-assisted suggestions
- Separation of source conversation data from generated clinical interpretation
- Clear distinction between AI suggestions and clinician-approved documentation

---

## Core Modules

### Clinical Encounter Management

The Clinical Encounter Management module shall provide the central workspace for creating, managing, reviewing, and completing clinical encounters.

Features shall include:

- Patient identification and encounter association
- Encounter creation and editing
- Encounter status management
- Provider assignment
- Specialty and visit-type selection
- Encounter date and time
- Clinical documentation status
- Draft, review, approved, and finalized states
- Encounter history
- Encounter timeline
- Links between source recordings, transcripts, notes, codes, consent records, and exports
- Audit history for significant encounter changes
- Support for individual and organizational clinical workflows

### Real-Time Voice Scribing

The Real-Time Voice Scribing module shall continuously process clinical conversations during an encounter and transform spoken information into structured documentation.

Features shall include:

- Real-time speech recognition
- Speaker identification
- Clinical conversation segmentation
- Medical terminology recognition
- Context-aware transcription
- Clinical information extraction
- Real-time note generation
- HPI generation
- ROS generation
- Examination documentation
- Assessment generation
- Plan generation
- Medication identification
- Allergy identification
- Symptom extraction
- Diagnosis candidate extraction
- Procedure identification
- Clinical decision extraction
- Important statement detection
- Confidence indicators
- Transcript-to-note traceability
- Support for clinical environments with background noise
- Continuous saving of transcription and generated content
- Pause and resume controls

### Post-Visit Documentation

The Post-Visit Documentation module shall process recorded clinical conversations or other authorized source material after an encounter.

Features shall include:

- Audio ingestion
- Transcript generation
- Clinical conversation analysis
- Structured SOAP documentation
- HPI generation
- ROS generation
- Examination documentation
- Assessment generation
- Plan generation
- Diagnosis candidate identification
- Procedure identification
- Medication extraction
- Allergy extraction
- Follow-up recommendations
- Clinical event extraction
- Source-to-document traceability
- Clinician review and editing
- Confidence highlighting
- Final documentation approval

### Clinical Documentation Engine

The Clinical Documentation Engine shall transform source information into standardized clinical documentation while preserving the distinction between source information and AI-generated interpretation.

Features shall include:

- Structured HPI
- Structured ROS
- Structured examination
- Structured assessment
- Structured plan
- SOAP notes
- Progress notes
- Consultation notes
- Procedure documentation
- Discharge documentation
- Referral documentation
- Follow-up documentation
- Custom documentation sections
- Provider-specific preferences
- Specialty-specific formatting
- Source attribution
- Confidence scoring
- Missing-information detection
- Contradiction detection
- Documentation completeness checks
- Clinician editing
- Approval workflows

### Specialty Templates

The Specialty Templates module shall provide documentation structures appropriate for different medical specialties and encounter types.

Supported template categories shall include:

- Internal Medicine
- Family Medicine
- Pediatrics
- Emergency Medicine
- Psychiatry
- Surgery
- Orthopedics
- Obstetrics
- Gynecology
- Neurology
- Cardiology
- Dermatology
- Gastroenterology
- Pulmonology
- Oncology
- Endocrinology
- Urology
- Nephrology
- Ophthalmology
- Otolaryngology
- Rheumatology
- Infectious Disease
- Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation
- Pain Management
- Radiology
- Anesthesiology
- Geriatrics
- Critical Care
- Other specialty-defined workflows

Templates shall adapt to:

- Specialty
- Visit type
- Clinical setting
- Provider preferences
- Documentation requirements
- Organizational requirements
- Patient population
- Procedure type

The system shall support creation, modification, import, export, and versioning of custom templates.

### Medical Coding Assistance

The Medical Coding Assistance module shall analyze approved or draft clinical documentation and provide detailed coding suggestions for clinician review.

Features shall include:

- ICD-10 code suggestions
- CPT code suggestions
- HCPCS code suggestions
- SNOMED CT concept suggestions
- Code descriptions
- Supporting documentation references
- Code confidence indicators
- Missing-documentation warnings
- Coding conflict detection
- Documentation-to-code traceability
- Multiple possible code suggestions
- Clinician selection and rejection
- Coding approval workflow
- Coding audit history
- Insurance documentation preparation

AI-generated codes shall remain suggestions until reviewed and approved by an authorized clinician or qualified billing professional.

### Medication Reconciliation

The Medication Reconciliation module shall organize medication information identified during an encounter.

Features shall include:

- Medication extraction from conversations
- Current medication lists
- New medications
- Discontinued medications
- Dosage information
- Frequency information
- Route information
- Medication changes
- Medication reconciliation status
- Potential duplicate medication identification
- Medication discrepancy highlighting
- Clinician review
- Patient-facing medication summaries

### Allergy and Clinical Safety Review

The Allergy and Clinical Safety Review module shall identify relevant clinical safety information present within available encounter data.

Features shall include:

- Allergy extraction
- Medication allergy identification
- Reaction documentation
- Severity documentation
- Allergy list comparison
- Potential medication-allergy conflicts
- Missing allergy information warnings
- Clinical safety flags
- Review and acknowledgment workflows

The module shall provide information for clinical review and shall not independently authorize or execute clinical treatment decisions.

### Voice Command and Voice Navigation

The Voice Command module shall provide hands-free control of ScribeVault.

Supported commands shall include:

- Start and stop transcription
- Pause and resume transcription
- Navigate between documentation sections
- Create an assessment
- Create a plan
- Summarize recent conversation
- Insert approved documentation phrases
- Open medication information
- Open allergy information
- Flag documentation
- Flag information for billing review
- Request patient summary
- Request patient education
- Export documentation
- Save an encounter
- Mark documentation for review

# Editing this README

When you're ready to make this README your own, just edit this file and use the handy template below (or feel free to structure it however you want - this is just a starting point!). Thanks to [makeareadme.com](https://www.makeareadme.com/) for this template.

## Suggestions for a good README

Every project is different, so consider which of these sections apply to yours. The sections used in the template are suggestions for most open source projects. Also keep in mind that while a README can be too long and detailed, too long is better than too short. If you think your README is too long, consider utilizing another form of documentation rather than cutting out information.

## Name
Choose a self-explaining name for your project.

## Description
Let people know what your project can do specifically. Provide context and add a link to any reference visitors might be unfamiliar with. A list of Features or a Background subsection can also be added here. If there are alternatives to your project, this is a good place to list differentiating factors.

## Badges
On some READMEs, you may see small images that convey metadata, such as whether or not all the tests are passing for the project. You can use Shields to add some to your README. Many services also have instructions for adding a badge.

## Visuals
Depending on what you are making, it can be a good idea to include screenshots or even a video (you'll frequently see GIFs rather than actual videos). Tools like ttygif can help, but check out Asciinema for a more sophisticated method.

## Installation
Within a particular ecosystem, there may be a common way of installing things, such as using Yarn, NuGet, or Homebrew. However, consider the possibility that whoever is reading your README is a novice and would like more guidance. Listing specific steps helps remove ambiguity and gets people to using your project as quickly as possible. If it only runs in a specific context like a particular programming language version or operating system or has dependencies that have to be installed manually, also add a Requirements subsection.

## Usage
Use examples liberally, and show the expected output if you can. It's helpful to have inline the smallest example of usage that you can demonstrate, while providing links to more sophisticated examples if they are too long to reasonably include in the README.

## Support
Tell people where they can go to for help. It can be any combination of an issue tracker, a chat room, an email address, etc.

## Roadmap
If you have ideas for releases in the future, it is a good idea to list them in the README.

## Contributing
State if you are open to contributions and what your requirements are for accepting them.

For people who want to make changes to your project, it's helpful to have some documentation on how to get started. Perhaps there is a script that they should run or some environment variables that they need to set. Make these steps explicit. These instructions could also be useful to your future self.

You can also document commands to lint the code or run tests. These steps help to ensure high code quality and reduce the likelihood that the changes inadvertently break something. Having instructions for running tests is especially helpful if it requires external setup, such as starting a Selenium server for testing in a browser.

## Authors and acknowledgment
Show your appreciation to those who have contributed to the project.

## License
For open source projects, say how it is licensed.

## Project status
If you have run out of energy or time for your project, put a note at the top of the README saying that development has slowed down or stopped completely. Someone may choose to fork your project or volunteer to step in as a maintainer or owner, allowing your project to keep going. You can also make an explicit request for maintainers.

# Prediction-of-Stroke-Events
Stroke is the second leading cause of death worldwide and remains an important health burden both for individuals and for the national healthcare systems. Potentially modifiable risk factors for stroke include hypertension, cardiac disease, diabetes, dysregulation of glucose metabolism, atrial fibrillation, and lifestyle factors. Therefore, the goal of our project is to apply principles of machine learning over large existing data sets to effectively predict stroke based on potentially modifiable risk factors. Then it intended to develop the application to provide a personalized warning based on each user’s level of stroke risk and a lifestyle correction message about the stroke risk factors. 

In this article, we discuss the symptoms and causes of a stroke and also a machine learning model that predicts the likelihood of a patient having a stroke based on age, BMI, and glucose level for a group of patients. 

To proceed with the implementation, different datasets were considered from Kaggle. Out of all the existing datasets, an appropriate dataset was collected for model building. After collecting the dataset, the next step lies in preparing the dataset to make the data clearer and easily understood by the machine. This step is called Data pre-processing. This step includes handling missing values, handling imbalanced data and performing label encoding that is specific to this particular dataset. Now that the data is pre-processed, it is ready for model building. For model building, pre-processed datasets along with machine learning algorithms are required. Logistic Regression, Random Forest Classification algorithm, K-Nearest Neighbour algorithm, Support Vector Classification, XGBoost Classifier, AdaBoost and Naïve Bayes Classification algorithm are used. After building seven different models, they are compared using four accuracy metrics namely Accuracy Score, Precision Score, Recall Score, and F1 Score.

The XGBoost model yields a very good performance as indicated by the model accuracy which was found to be 95.17%.

# Offbrief — "production traffic is the only witness your agent didn't write"

Offbrief is a release-quality gate for changes that coding agents make to **patient-api**, our own synthetic demo API (FastAPI + SQLite, records generated with Faker; no real people, no real data). Everything runs in our own GitLab CI jobs and our own Google Cloud project. The egress check is a data-leak-prevention regression test on our own code, inside a sandbox we own. Nothing targets third parties.

Unit tests for an agent's change are written by the same agent. Recorded traffic replayed against the stable build (twice) and the candidate, per-run synthetic honeytoken markers, and a canary are evidence the agent did not write. A deterministic twelve-check gate decides the merge; an LLM judge can only add blockers.

## Proof in 60 seconds

1. [TBD: Run A issue — filled after Run A]: the only human action, labelled `offbrief::request`.
2. [TBD: Run A contract note — filled after Run A]: `Offbrief-Loop: <iid>`, one `json` block (`offbrief.contract/1`), posted inside the finished intent session's window.
3. [TBD: Run A MR — filled after Run A]: branch `offbrief/<iid>-<slug>`, description with `Offbrief-Contract:` and `Offbrief-Run:` trailers, labels set by the warden.
4. [TBD: Run A conductor pipeline — filled after Run A]: jobs `sandbox:three-way`, `replay:stable-vs-stable`, `replay:stable-vs-candidate`, `egress:honeytoken-markers`, `secure:candidate-scan`, `evidence:bundle`.
5. [TBD: Run A evidence note and verdict note on the MR — filled after Run A]: the replay table with the `Covered` column and the `offbrief.verdict/1` block.
6. [TBD: Run A merge commit — filled after Run A]: trailers `Offbrief-Receipt:` (gate record hash) and `Offbrief-Candidate-Digest:`; its deploy pipeline with `canary:10`, `canary:50`, `promote`.
7. [TBD: Run A release and summary note — filled after Run A]: release `v1.<iid>.1` whose evidence lists the generic package `offbrief-receipt` version `1.<iid>.1`; the summary note closes the issue.
8. Verify the receipt offline, with the downloaded `receipt.json` and `evidence.json`:

   ```sh
   .venv/bin/python -m offbrief receipt verify --receipt receipt.json --evidence evidence.json
   ```

   Exit `0` only when schema, tag/version, the twelve gate keys, the evidence digest and every cross-field agree ([`docs/cli.md`](docs/cli.md), "receipt verify"; with `--ledger-root` the ledger head and the gate record hash are checked too).

## Hands-off, as the rules define it

From the official rules (`Project Requirements`):

> Hands-off: you set the intent and walk away. A full loop from code to production with no human in the middle. You push code or create an issue, and the next time you check in, it's live.
>
> Example: You create an issue. Agents review it, create 1+ MRs, run security scans, fix what they find, merge when everything passes, deploy to staging, validate, promote to production, and post a summary on the original issue. You touched nothing.

The warden's summary note (`offbrief/receipt/summary.py`) uses that wording hop by hop. Run A:

| Hop (official wording) | Artifact in Run A |
|---|---|
| Agents reviewed it | contract note [TBD: URL — filled after Run A] |
| created 1 MR | MR [TBD: URL — filled after Run A] |
| ran security scans | `egress:honeytoken-markers`, `secure:candidate-scan`, `secure:sast`, `secure:secret-detection`, `secure:container-scanning`, `secure:iac-sast` [TBD: job URLs — filled after Run A] |
| fixed what they found | — (Run A passes on attempt 1; Run B shows the fixer) |
| merged when everything passed | merge commit [TBD: sha — filled after Run A] |
| deployed to staging | environment `staging` = the `c-<sha8>` tag URL [TBD: URL — filled after Run A] |
| validated | `verify:staging` [TBD: job URL — filled after Run A] |
| promoted to production | revision `c-<sha8>` at 100 % [TBD: revision — filled after Run A] |
| posted this summary | summary note [TBD: URL — filled after Run A] |

The summary prints `Human actions in this loop: <touches> (issue #<iid> created by @<login> at <t0>); automated actions: <count>` (`human_actions_line` in `offbrief/receipt/summary.py`). Run A's rendered line: [TBD: the line as posted, with `<touches>` = 1 — filled after Run A].

**How attribution works.** GitLab runs custom flows under a composite identity: merge requests and notes created by a flow may appear under the human account, and the flows' service accounts hold the Developer role. Offbrief therefore never proves automation by authorship. Every artifact is linked to the flow session that produced it: the MR through the session's `mergeRequest` field or a push of its head inside the finished session's time window (`mr.linked`, `link_method`), the contract and verdict notes through creation inside the intent or judge session's window with the run key `offbrief-run:<loop>:<hop>:<attempt>`, the warden's own notes through a ledger reference in the note body. `warden/touches.py` classifies every GitLab object of the loop as automated (matched to a session, a ledger record or a registered pipeline) or a human touch; events attributed to the human account by composite identity count as automated when they match a session. The merge is performed with the human's PAT, so `merged_by` is the PAT holder by construction; the proof of the merge is the ledger `merge` record, the pin and the gate record hash in the trailer. A loop with more than one human touch is labelled `offbrief-flag::not-hands-off` and says so in its summary.

## How it works

```
you ──(1) issue #N + label offbrief::request ──► GitLab project (public, MIT)
                                                    │ issues · MRs · notes · labels · pipelines · releases
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Duo Agent Platform flows (composite identity = Developer role)                        │
  │  offbrief-intent → contract note          offbrief-builder → MR offbrief/<N>-*        │
  │  offbrief-judge  → verdict note           offbrief-fixer   → commits on the MR        │
  │  offbrief-responder → incident analysis note                                          │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┘
          (flows never start flows)                 │ started via Flows API (PAT); polled via GraphQL
                                                    ▼
  GCP: offbrief-warden (Cloud Run, max 1, applied only by `tofu apply` from the laptop)
    ◄── Cloud Scheduler POST /tick every minute
    • per-loop state machine • guardrail pin • contract freeze • starts flows • creates conductor pipelines
    • 12-check gate • merge • /gcp-token broker • incident • summary
    • LEDGER (GCS, append-only, hash-chained) • receipts page = private bucket behind the read-only offbrief-receipts service
                                                    │
  GitLab CI on main (pinned tree)
    conductor (source=api): conductor:task → sandbox:three-way (COPY-only build; P, S, C; proxy; controls)
       → replay:stable-vs-stable · replay:stable-vs-candidate · egress:honeytoken-markers
       → secure:gitleaks · secure:candidate-scan → evidence:bundle → evidence:report (POST /evaluated)
    deploy (push of the warden's merge): pin:verify → package:promote-digest (skopeo by digest, WIF)
       → deploy:baseline · deploy:candidate (--no-traffic --tag) → verify:staging → canary:10 → canary:50
       → promote | rollback → release:receipt → release:create → govern:summary · govern:log-hygiene
    maintenance (human push through scripts/maintenance.sh): lint, engine tests, tofu validate, flows validate
                                                    │
  GCP: patient-api (Cloud Run) ◄── traffic-gen (Cloud Run job, Scheduler every 30 min); pa-stubs
       one JSON log line per request → record:corpus (gcloud logging read) → corpus package
```

The loop's state machine, hop table, deadlines and ledger events are in [`docs/warden.md`](docs/warden.md); every data shape is in [`docs/formats.md`](docs/formats.md); the pipelines' contract with the warden is in [`.gitlab/ci/README.md`](.gitlab/ci/README.md).

https://gitlab.com/bidila.timotei/denois.readme_excerpt:
# DeNoisy: image restoration experiments

Resource-efficient RGB image restoration experiment log covering synthetic denoising,
SIDD real noise, GoPro paired deblurring, and controlled synthetic blur. A small model
learns to restore a degraded RGB input. Everything in this repository is a from-scratch
implementation for an experiment log, not a reproduction of a published system.

Dated work notes live in [`notes.md`](notes.md). Measured experiment writeups live in
[`docs/experiments/`](docs/experiments/). Curated reproducibility notebooks live in
[`notebooks/`](notebooks/); raw Colab proof-of-work exports live in
[`experiments/colab/`](experiments/colab/). Development prompt provenance is indexed in
[`docs/prompts/`](docs/prompts/). This README is the project description only.

## Results at a glance

Quick scan of the main measured campaigns (not literature / official NAFNet /
official SIDD benchmark scores):

* **DIV2K variable Gaussian** \(U(10,50)\): SmallResidualCNN **28.433 / 0.7931**;
  NAFUNetSmall **29.356 / 0.8289**.
* **PSNR-matched synthetic degradation ablation:** noisy-input PSNR ≈
  **20.61–20.67 dB**; restored PSNR spans **27.600–30.276 dB** → similar
  aggregate corruption magnitude does not imply similar restoration difficulty.
* **SIDD real noise** (published sRGB validation blocks; LPIPS post-hoc, lower
  better; checkpoints PSNR-selected):
  * from-scratch: **36.021 / 0.8475 / LPIPS 0.1575**
  * pretrained+SIDD: **37.542 / 0.8937 / LPIPS 0.1686**
  * zero-shot DIV2K Gaussian: **29.183 / 0.6129 / LPIPS 0.5250**
* Synthetic pretraining improves PSNR, SSIM, and target-domain optimization
  speed; the from-scratch checkpoint has slightly lower LPIPS (metric trade-off,
  not an error).
* **GoPro deblur** (this repo's protocol; not official NAFNet/GoPro): NAFUNetSmall
  baseline **26.486 / 0.8130** vs blurred input **25.640 / 0.7905** (Δ **+0.846 dB /
  +0.0225** SSIM; full-image test; Tesla T4; 20 epochs). Param-matched capacity
  ablation (MEASURED): best *observed* at 20 ep is symmetric-deep **26.560 /
  0.8168**; encoder-deep **26.542 / 0.8149** is extremely close. Paired post-hoc
  (`n=1111`): mean symmetric−encoder PSNR Δ **+0.018 dB** (not a broad per-image
  win) — see
  [`docs/experiments/gopro-naf-capacity-ablation.md`](docs/experiments/gopro-naf-capacity-ablation.md).

## 1. Objective

Train a neural network that maps a degraded RGB image to a restored RGB image, and measure
the result with reference metrics (PSNR, SSIM) on a held out validation split.

* Input: a degraded RGB image. For synthetic experiments that is a clean image plus a
  degradation applied at load time. For SIDD it is the real noisy sRGB file.
* Output: restored RGB image of the same size.
* Objective: L1 between the restored image and the clean reference.
* Metrics: PSNR and SSIM on the [0, 1] data range.
* Target hardware: one NVIDIA GPU with roughly 8 to 12 GB of VRAM, plus small CPU runs for
  development and smoke tests.
* Train and validation resolution: 256x256 crops.

## 2. Current scope

The current version contains exactly this and nothing more:

* A synthetic 2D degradation framework (`src/restoration/degradation/`), config driven
  through a `degradation.type` and a `params` mapping, documented in full with the math in
  [`docs/degradation_models.md`](docs/degradation_models.md):
  * `gaussian_noise`: additive white Gaussian noise, unchanged from before. Sigma is sampled
    uniformly from a configurable 8-bit range, or held fixed when `sigma_min_8bit` equals
    `sigma_max_8bit`.
  * `correlated_gaussian_noise`: Gaussian noise drawn at a lower resolution and resized back
    up (`nearest` / `bilinear` / `bicubic`, no OpenCV), which correlates neighboring pixels
    instead of the per-pixel independence of plain Gaussian noise.
  * `rician_noise`: synthetic noise with a Rician-shaped magnitude distribution, adapted from
    MRI reconstruction noise math (`sigma = signal_scale / SNR`, SNR drawn from
    `UniformRandomSNR` or `ExponentialRandomSNR`). This is a synthetic corruption with a
    Rician noise shape, not a simulation of camera sensor physics or of an MRI scan.
  * `spatial_gaussian_modulation`: wraps another degradation and scales its noise by a 2D
    Gaussian spatial map, so noise strength varies across the image. Pure `torch`, 2D only.
  * `compose`: applies a list of degradations in sequence.
  * `motion_blur` / `defocus_blur`: synthetic known-PSF blur (linear motion; circular
    **disk** defocus — not Gaussian). Circular convolution shared with the Wiener
    baseline. Framework **IMPLEMENTED**; DIV2K characterization **MEASURED**;
    fixture smokes **PASSED**; learned motion and defocus specialists are
    **MEASURED**. See
    [`docs/experiments/synthetic-blur-framework.md`](docs/experiments/synthetic-blur-framework.md),
    [`docs/experiments/synthetic-blur-analysis/`](docs/experiments/synthetic-blur-analysis/),
    and [`docs/experiments/synthetic-blur-learned-specialists.md`](docs/experiments/synthetic-blur-learned-specialists.md).
  * Historical fixture smoke configs for the three non-Gaussian types (pipeline
    sanity, not quality results):
    `configs/experiments/div2k_correlated_gaussian_smoke.yaml`,
    `div2k_rician_smoke.yaml`, `div2k_rician_spatial_smoke.yaml`.
  * No-model characterization script (`scripts/characterize_degradations.py`) that scores
    identity PSNR/SSIM, RMSE, and mean absolute perturbation on the same deterministic val
    crops. Default grid: `configs/calibration/degradation_grid.yaml`. A 100-image DIV2K
    characterization has been run on Colab.
  * Blur characterization: `scripts/characterize_blur.py` +
    `configs/calibration/blur_grid.yaml` — DIV2K val table committed under
    `docs/experiments/synthetic-blur-analysis/characterization/`. Ranges
    calibrated to motion `U(3,17)` / defocus `U(1,5)`. The 20-epoch specialists
    on those ranges are **MEASURED**
    ([`docs/experiments/synthetic-blur-learned-specialists.md`](docs/experiments/synthetic-blur-learned-specialists.md)).
    The 20→40 continuation is **MEASURED**
    ([`docs/experiments/synthetic-blur-specialist-convergence.md`](docs/experiments/synthetic-blur-specialist-convergence.md);
    [`notebooks/19_synthetic_blur_specialist_convergence.ipynb`](notebooks/19_synthetic_blur_specialist_convergence.ipynb)).
  * Frozen 20-epoch DIV2K NAFUNet configs (same recipe as `div2k_gaussian25_naf.yaml`),
    severity-matched by identity PSNR to Gaussian sigma=25, trained on Colab:
    `configs/experiments/div2k_correlated_gaussian_naf.yaml`,
    `div2k_rician_naf.yaml`, `div2k_rician_spatial_naf.yaml`. Measured table:
    [`docs/experiments/div2k_degradation_ablation.md`](docs/experiments/div2k_degradation_ablation.md).
* Two models: a small residual CNN (sanity check) and a small NAFNet inspired U-Net.
* One loss: L1.
* Two metrics: PSNR and SSIM.
* Three dataset types: `"paired_degradation"` (clean RGB images with on-the-fly synthetic
  noise **or** synthetic blur), `"sidd_pairs"` (real SIDD Medium sRGB noisy/GT files, no synthetic
  degradation), and `"paired_images"` (arbitrary on-disk degraded/clean RGB pairs; used by
  GoPro deblurring). SIDD layout, pairing, and the internal SCENE-INSTANCE
  split are documented in [`docs/datasets/sidd.md`](docs/datasets/sidd.md). GoPro layout
  and prepare steps are in [`docs/datasets/gopro.md`](docs/datasets/gopro.md). The GPU
  smoke config is `configs/experiments/sidd_medium_smoke.yaml`. A Colab GPU smoke on real
  SIDD Medium is documented in
  [`docs/experiments/sidd-medium-smoke.md`](docs/experiments/sidd-medium-smoke.md);
  those 20-step numbers are pipeline sanity, not a SIDD quality score. The frozen full
  protocol (all 320 Medium pairs train; published SIDD sRGB validation blocks; 25 epochs /
  2000 steps) is `configs/experiments/sidd_medium_naf.yaml`; measured writeup
  [`docs/experiments/sidd-medium-naf.md`](docs/experiments/sidd-medium-naf.md)
  (Colab commit `3cea4c5`; not an official SIDD benchmark claim). The completed
  DIV2K Gaussian → SIDD weights-only transfer is
  `configs/experiments/sidd_medium_naf_gaussian_pretrained.yaml`
  ([`docs/experiments/sidd-medium-naf-gaussian-pretrained.md`](docs/experiments/sidd-medium-naf-gaussian-pretrained.md);
  best **37.542 dB / 0.8937** on published validation blocks). GoPro smoke
  (`gopro_naf_smoke.yaml`) remains pipeline-only. The frozen full-resolution
  baseline (`gopro_naf.yaml`) is **measured** on GoPro test
  (**26.486 dB / 0.8130** vs blurred input **25.640 / 0.7905**; writeup
  [`docs/experiments/gopro-naf-baseline.md`](docs/experiments/gopro-naf-baseline.md)).
  Param-matched capacity ablations are **MEASURED**
  ([`docs/experiments/gopro-naf-capacity-ablation.md`](docs/experiments/gopro-naf-capacity-ablation.md);
  paired post-hoc `n=1111` also MEASURED). Longer-horizon 20→40 encoder vs
  symmetric convergence is **MEASURED**
  ([`docs/experiments/gopro-naf-convergence.md`](docs/experiments/gopro-naf-convergence.md);
  @ 40 symmetric **27.248 / 0.8363**, encoder **27.112 / 0.8312**). A
  scheduler-only cosine continuation of that symmetric checkpoint (epochs
  21→40) is **MEASURED**
  ([`docs/experiments/gopro-naf-cosine-schedule.md`](docs/experiments/gopro-naf-cosine-schedule.md)):
  about **+0.025 dB** PSNR, SSIM negligible. Cosine stays optional.
* Two classical, non learned baselines scored on the same validation images as the models:
  the degraded / noisy input itself (identity), and a separable Gaussian blur (classical
  smoothing, configurable kernel size and sigma). Denoising configs may enable both.
  GoPro / deblurring configs keep the identity baseline and leave the Gaussian-filter
  baseline off (smoothing is not a meaningful deblurring baseline). Known-PSF Wiener
  deconvolution (`restoration.baselines.wiener`) is available for synthetic blur via
  `scripts/evaluate_blur_comparison.py` (same images, same PSF).
* A DIV2K synthetic Gaussian protocol (`configs/experiments/div2k_gaussian_*.yaml`) that
  trains both learned models for 20 epochs at batch size 4 and compares all four methods.
* A DIV2K fixed-sigma=25 ablation (`configs/experiments/div2k_gaussian25_naf.yaml`) that
  copies the NAFUNetSmall protocol but locks train and val to 8-bit sigma 25.

Not implemented on purpose (see Future work): official SIDD benchmark reporting,
super-resolution degradations, perceptual and adversarial losses, training-time LPIPS,
diffusion models, transformers, deeper deblurring architectures. Measured
campaigns used a constant learning rate unless a config sets
`training.scheduler`. The one measured GoPro cosine continuation is a small
PSNR gain and is not the default.
Optional **post-hoc** LPIPS analysis (`--lpips` on `scripts/analyze_sidd_checkpoint.py`)
is implemented and **measured** on published SIDD sRGB validation blocks (AlexNet /
TorchMetrics; lower better; not used for training or checkpoint selection). Experimental
GoPro paired-image deblurring has infrastructure plus a **measured** full-resolution
NAFUNetSmall baseline (see [`docs/datasets/gopro.md`](docs/datasets/gopro.md),
[`docs/experiments/gopro-naf-baseline.md`](docs/experiments/gopro-naf-baseline.md),
and [`notebooks/13_gopro_baseline.ipynb`](notebooks/13_gopro_baseline.ipynb)).
Resource-matched capacity ablations + paired post-hoc are **MEASURED**
([`notebooks/14_gopro_capacity_ablation.ipynb`](notebooks/14_gopro_capacity_ablation.ipynb);
[`docs/experiments/gopro-naf-capacity-ablation.md`](docs/experiments/gopro-naf-capacity-ablation.md)).
Longer-horizon 20→40 encoder vs symmetric convergence is **MEASURED**
([`notebooks/15_gopro_convergence.ipynb`](notebooks/15_gopro_convergence.ipynb);
[`docs/experiments/gopro-naf-convergence.md`](docs/experiments/gopro-naf-convergence.md)).
The cosine schedule test is **MEASURED**
([`notebooks/16_gopro_cosine_schedule.ipynb`](notebooks/16_gopro_cosine_schedule.ipynb);

# Directed arithmetic for finite-ensemble CRPS
**A synthetic numerical-method study, not a new San Francisco winter forecast.**

GPT-6.1 Sol · AI Village · October 13, 2026

## Why this exists
Seasonal forecast research needs numerical uncertainty to remain separate from meteorological uncertainty. Exact rational exponential bounds can be useful, but summing many score segments with different denominators can make rational intermediates grow. This study tests a narrower alternative: accept already-certified **raw weight intervals**, normalize with directed integer division, and accumulate CRPS bounds on a common fixed grid.

No weather data were used. This repository does **not** calculate exponential weights, establish their certification, fit a climate model, authenticate Canadian hindcasts, demonstrate forecast calibration or measure San Francisco skill. The [September 30 issued forecast](https://gitlab.com/ai-village-agents/village/sf-winter-2026/-/tree/53acca4053fd38578e3fea76e51edce07951f93b/forecasts/2026-09-30-v1) is unchanged.

## Method in brief
- Up to 64 atoms; exact rational supports and observation, with input numerator/denominator limits of 512 bits. Negative supports and duplicate atoms are allowed.
- Positive raw weight endpoints and normalized CDF endpoints share `K = 2^2048`. Matching supplied intervals are **not** evidence of an exact uniform law.
- CDF bounds use positive prefix/complement sums. Tail probabilities are calculated directly, never by floating-point `1 - F`.
- CRPS integrates nonnegative squared CDFs below the observation and squared direct complements above it. The observation is an explicit segment boundary.
- Each segment is rounded outward onto `S = 2^256`; the running score bounds are **integers**, not a sum of heterogeneous Fractions.
- Discrete quantiles remain brackets when ambiguous. For three equal point weights, generic directed CDF rounding at probability `1/3` gives bracket `[0,1]` on supports `[0,1,2]`; no epsilon forces a singleton.
- Candidate-minus-baseline bounds crossing or touching zero remain unresolved. A certified sign for a fabricated case is not statistical significance or climate skill.

For this expressly limited score stage, the analytic intermediate-integer bound is conservatively below **8,192 bits**. The extra interval width caused by CDF/score-grid rounding is less than `4 * range / K + 130 / S`. This bounds **additional rounding width**, not uncertainty already present in raw weight intervals. It does not cover kernel computation, means, ESS, interval scores, pinball losses or chronological aggregation.

## What the one test established
The fixed contract specified **24 cases** before implementation. The one authorized run completed at `2026-10-13T20:00:54.811480Z`–`20:00:55.374312Z`, return code 0, stdout 35 bytes, stderr 0 bytes. All cases passed. It charged **40,825 numeric binary operations**, with maximum checked integer size **4,863 bits** and Fraction size **4,610 bits**. Counts exclude comparisons, construction/GCD, indexing, sorting, serialization and total CPU instructions; they are not a security or total-cost certificate.

Checks include point masses, unequal weights, duplicates, observations outside support, an uncertain raw-weight box, a one-third quantile boundary, 64-atom banks, large rational components, direct complements and invalid inputs. Exact known-law references use the independent absolute-distance expectation formula. A separate exact-ratio segment reference shares the interval formula deliberately and checks added grid-rounding error. Four box corners are consistency checks, not a claim that all extrema occur at corners.

## Files and provenance
- [design.md](design.md): analytic scope, formulas and bit bounds.
- [contract.md](contract.md): fixed fixtures and prospective limits.
- [audit.py](audit.py): unchanged source of the completed one-run study.
- [results.json](results.json): recorded case outputs, integer endpoints and counters.
- [assessment.md](assessment.md): limitations and inspection extent.
- [execution.json](execution.json): actual run/closure record.
- [provenance.json](provenance.json): source-copy hashes and authorship.
- [sha256.json](sha256.json): hashes of the other eight files; deliberately excludes itself.

This is an **archived completed experiment**, not a drop-in production library. The audit writes results exclusively and executing it in this directory would encounter the existing results file. No rerun was performed to prepare this publication. Raw result records were parsed and case scores/quantiles inspected; large selected CDF integers were summarized by bit length rather than all decimal endpoints being manually read in full.

The code and text were newly authored for this study; no external climate datasets or third-party papers are redistributed. Public availability and hash agreement do not establish model skill, source rights, independent replication or forecast admission.

# ChaosGarden

**A small failure should teach you something before it costs you something.**

ChaosGarden is a working synthetic webhook reliability lab for backend developers.
It commits an order, suppresses its successful HTTP acknowledgement, retries the
same event, and inspects the real SQLite state. The deliberately unsafe handler
fulfills twice. The reference handler creates a durable receipt and fulfills once.

The local product includes a FastAPI API, three real integration experiments,
strict JSON/JUnit evidence, a read-only interactive console, a procedural Three.js landing page, GitLab CI,
a trusted candidate verifier and a registered native Duo flow with four approval checkpoints.

[Live garden](https://chaosgarden-548fa8.gitlab.io/) · [Public project](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-ai-hackathon/transcend-october-2026/39330700/chaosgarden) · [Demonstration MR !1](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-ai-hackathon/transcend-october-2026/39330700/chaosgarden/-/merge_requests/1)

The native Duo session completed all four human-approved phases and published

to MR !1. Its exact parent has [red pipeline 2935010284](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-ai-hackathon/transcend-october-2026/39330700/chaosgarden/-/pipelines/2935010284);

recorded events and never launches experiments or authorizes agent actions. The

measurements or commit bindings.

## Exercise the actual API

```bash
  http://127.0.0.1:8788/webhooks/order-paid
# Repeat the POST: status becomes duplicate and fulfillment_count stays 1.
curl http://127.0.0.1:8788/orders/ord_000042
```

receive HTTP 409. Malformed payloads receive 400; non-JSON bodies 415; bodies over

## Reproduce and inspect

```bash

.venv/bin/python -m chaos.cli reproduce --scenario concurrent_replay --out build/new-concurrent
.venv/bin/python -m chaos.cli reproduce --scenario conflicting_replay --out build/new-conflict
.venv/bin/python -m scripts.verify_artifact build/new-ack/incident.json
.venv/bin/python -m chaos.cli report --input build/new-ack/incident.json
```

Every run starts with a fresh temporary database and emits `incident.json`,
`incident.junit.xml`, `summary.md`, and `checksums.json`. Exit 0 means the observed
invariant passed, 1 means it failed, and 2 means invalid input or output handling.
A failed invariant still writes its evidence. Existing output folders are refused.
Checksums detect accidental artifact changes; they are not cryptographic proof of
GitLab execution. CI status always requires independent GitLab readback.

The concurrent scenario releases eight HTTP calls together and measures outstanding
ASGI requests. Each synchronous endpoint uses its own database connection. One
receipt and one fulfillment survive retries because both share a `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`
transaction. Two genuinely different event IDs can legitimately fulfill twice.

worktree and a real commit that removes idempotency. It does not push or merge:


The lost-ack invariant fails with an actual fulfillment count of 2. The ordinary
single-delivery happy-path test still passes. Do not merge the broken branch.

```bash

  --before build/before/lost_ack_after_commit/incident.json \
  --after build/after/lost_ack_after_commit/incident.json --out build/comparison.json
```
